text:
The model in code
The model of this chapter is supply and demand in the labor market. Employment \(L\) goes on the horizontal axis and the wage \(w\) on the vertical axis, so we write each curve as “the wage at each level of employment”:
\[\text{labor demand: } w = \bar{a}_d - \bar{b}_d\,L \qquad\qquad \text{labor supply: } w = \bar{a}_s + \bar{b}_s\,L\]

Labor demand slopes down. Firms hire until the extra output of the last worker (the marginal product of labor, Chapter 4) equals the wage, and each extra worker adds less than the one before.
Labor supply slopes up. A higher wage makes an hour of leisure more expensive, so more people choose to work.

The textbook draws these curves without numbers. We use simple illustrative values: \(\bar{a}_d = 100\), \(\bar{b}_d = 1\), \(\bar{a}_s = 10\), \(\bar{b}_s = 1\). Setting demand equal to supply gives the equilibrium
\[L^* = \frac{\bar{a}_d - \bar{a}_s}{\bar{b}_d + \bar{b}_s} \qquad\qquad w^* = \bar{a}_d - \bar{b}_d\,L^*\]
so \(L^* = 90/2 = 45\) and \(w^* = 55\).
Later we add an income tax at rate \(\tau\): firms pay \(w\), but workers keep only \((1-\tau)w\). Workers decide how much to work from the wage they keep, so supply becomes \((1-\tau)w = \bar{a}_s + \bar{b}_s L\). Solving with demand gives
\[L^* = \frac{(1-\tau)\,\bar{a}_d - \bar{a}_s}{(1-\tau)\,\bar{b}_d + \bar{b}_s}\]
which is the formula above when \(\tau = 0\). One function, equilibrium, covers both cases.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing a_d=100.0 gives the argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. A function can return two results at once, separated by a comma.


def labor_demand(L, a_d=100.0, b_d=1.0):
    """Figure 7.3: the wage firms are willing to pay when they employ L, w = a_d - b_d L."""
    return a_d - b_d * L


def labor_supply(L, a_s=10.0, b_s=1.0):
    """Figure 7.3: the wage workers need to receive to supply L, w = a_s + b_s L."""
    return a_s + b_s * L


def equilibrium(a_d=100.0, b_d=1.0, a_s=10.0, b_s=1.0, tau=0.0):
    """Figures 7.3-7.4: employment L* and the wage firms pay w*, when workers keep (1 - tau) w."""
    L_star = ((1 - tau) * a_d - a_s) / ((1 - tau) * b_d + b_s)
    w_star = labor_demand(L_star, a_d, b_d)
    return L_star, w_star


def demand_at_wage(w, a_d=100.0, b_d=1.0):
    """Figure 7.6: the employment firms want at a given wage w (labor demand solved for L)."""
    return (a_d - w) / b_d


def supply_at_wage(w, a_s=10.0, b_s=1.0):
    """Figure 7.6: the number of people who want to work at a given wage w (labor supply solved for L)."""
    return (w - a_s) / b_s

A quick check of the functions against the numbers above.

Python note. L_star, w_star = equilibrium() stores the two results in two variables. An f-string such as f"L* = {L_star:.1f}" inserts a value into a piece of text; :.1f means “one decimal”.


L_star, w_star = equilibrium()
print(f"Equilibrium:            L* = {L_star:.1f}, w* = {w_star:.1f}")
print(f"At L*, demand wage = {labor_demand(L_star):.1f} and supply wage = {labor_supply(L_star):.1f}: the market clears")
L_tax, w_tax = equilibrium(tau=0.25)
print(f"With a 25% income tax:  L' = {L_tax:.2f}, firms pay w' = {w_tax:.2f}, workers keep {0.75 * w_tax:.2f}")

Equilibrium:            L* = 45.0, w* = 55.0
At L*, demand wage = 55.0 and supply wage = 55.0: the market clears
With a 25% income tax:  L' = 37.14, firms pay w' = 62.86, workers keep 47.14


Two small drawing helpers save us from repeating the same lines in every figure. add_curve draws one curve; add_point marks an equilibrium with a dot, a label and dotted lines down to the axes.

Python note. np.linspace(0, 110, 111) creates 111 evenly spaced numbers from 0 to 110: the employment levels at which we compute each curve. go.Figure() starts an empty chart and add_trace adds one line or set of points to it. row and col are only needed in figures with several panels; None means “the only panel”.


L_grid = np.linspace(0, 110, 111)          # employment levels used to draw every curve


def add_curve(fig, w, name, color, dash="solid", row=None, col=None):
    """Draw one curve: the wage w at every employment level in L_grid (no legend entry if name is "")."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=L_grid, y=w, name=name, showlegend=(name != ""),
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)), row=row, col=col)


def add_point(fig, L_point, w_point, label, row=None, col=None):
    """Mark an equilibrium with a dot, a short label and dotted lines down to the axes."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, L_point, L_point], y=[w_point, w_point, 0], mode="lines", showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dot")), row=row, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[L_point], y=[w_point], mode="markers+text", text=[label], showlegend=False,
                             textposition="top center", textfont=dict(size=15),
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=11)), row=row, col=col)

Figure 1: The U.S. employment-population ratio
Goal. See the long-run trend and the recessions in the share of adults who work.
The employment-population ratio is the percentage of the population aged 16 and over that has a job. The data are monthly, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. A second small file lists the start (peak) and end (trough) month of every U.S. recession since the 1950s, as dated by the NBER.

Python note. pd.read_csv(...) reads a data file into a DataFrame, a table with named columns. parse_dates=["date"] turns text such as "2020-04-01" into real dates. .tail() shows the last five rows.


emp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig7-1.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough"])
emp.tail()

September 2025 is followed by November 2025: October 2025 is missing because the survey was not carried out during that autumn’s federal government shutdown. The chart simply joins the two months.
We will shade recessions in three charts, so we write the shading once, as a function.

Python note. A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each recession: zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough) hands over one (peak, trough) pair at a time. The if skips recessions that ended before the chart starts, and fig.add_vrect shades the band between two dates. px.area draws a line and fills the area below it. rangeslider_visible=True adds a small copy of the chart below the axis: drag its handles to zoom in on a period.


def shade_recessions(fig, start):
    """Shade every NBER recession (peak to trough) that ends after the date start."""
    for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
        if trough >= pd.Timestamp(start):
            fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)


fig = px.area(emp, x="date", y="emp_pop_ratio", hover_name="date",
              labels={"date": "Year", "emp_pop_ratio": "Employment-population ratio (percent)"},
              title="More adults work than in 1960, but every recession cuts employment")
fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=TEAL, width=2))
shade_recessions(fig, "1960-01-01")
fig.update_yaxes(range=[50, 66])
fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True)
fig.show()




                                
                                            




What to notice.

The trend rose from about 56 percent in 1960 to a peak of 64.7 percent in April 2000, and it has stayed below that peak ever since.
The ratio falls in every recession (the shaded bands). The falls after 2007 and in spring 2020 are by far the deepest.
The textbook’s figure ends in early 2023; our data go to September 2026.


Key numbers: the trend and the Great Recession

Python note. set_index("date") uses the dates as row labels, so ratio.loc["1960"] keeps every month of 1960 and ratio.loc["2009":"2012"] every month from 2009 to 2012. .idxmax() and .idxmin() give the row label (here, the month) of the largest and smallest value, and :%B %Y prints a date as “April 2000”.


ratio = emp.set_index("date").emp_pop_ratio
crisis = ratio.loc["2009":"2012"]
print(f"1960 average:            {ratio.loc['1960'].mean():.1f}%")
print(f"Peak:                    {ratio.max():.1f}% in {ratio.idxmax():%B %Y}")
print(f"December 2006:           {ratio.loc['2006-12-01']:.1f}%")
print(f"January 2010:            {ratio.loc['2010-01-01']:.1f}%  (lowest 2009-2012: {crisis.min():.1f}% in {crisis.idxmin():%B %Y})")
print(f"Fall, Dec. 2006 to Jan. 2010: {ratio.loc['2006-12-01'] - ratio.loc['2010-01-01']:.1f} points")
print(f"Covid low:               {ratio.min():.1f}% in {ratio.idxmin():%B %Y};  latest: {ratio.iloc[-1]:.1f}%")

Peak:                    64.7% in April 2000

The textbook’s numbers hold: 56 percent in 1960, 63.4 percent at the end of 2006, and a fall of about 5 points by early 2010 (58.5 percent in January 2010 in today’s data, against 58.4 in the textbook; the low point came later, in November 2010).


Key numbers: men and women
The textbook says that the rise in the ratio came entirely from women. A second file splits the ratio by sex. We average the months of each year to compare years.

Python note. groupby(emp_sex.date.dt.year).mean() collects the rows of each calendar year and averages them, and .loc[[1960, 2000, 2025]] picks three rows by their label.

fig = px.line(emp_sex, x="date", y=["men", "women"], hover_name="date",

fig.show()

Figure 2: The U.S. unemployment rate
Goal. See how unemployment jumps in recessions and falls in recoveries.
A person is unemployed when she has no job, has looked for one in the past four weeks, and is available to work. The labor force is everybody who is employed or unemployed, and the unemployment rate is the share of the labor force that is unemployed.

unrate = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig7-2.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
fig = px.area(unrate, x="date", y="unemployment_rate", hover_name="date",
              labels={"date": "Year", "unemployment_rate": "Unemployment rate (percent)"},
              title="Unemployment jumps in every recession and falls slowly afterwards")
fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2))
shade_recessions(fig, "1950-01-01")
fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 16])
fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True)
fig.show()




                                
                                            




What to notice.

Every shaded recession brings a jump in unemployment. The highest peaks are late 1982, October 2009 and April 2020.
The Covid-19 jump was the largest and the shortest: the rate fell back much faster than after 2009.
Between recessions, unemployment falls gradually, often for many years.


Key numbers: peaks and recoveries

title: Chapter 7: The Labor Market, Wages, and Unemployment
section: Figure 3: The labor market
text:
Figure 3: The labor market
Goal. Draw the supply-and-demand diagram of the labor market and see how its equilibrium moves.
Labor demand \(w = \bar{a}_d - \bar{b}_d L\) slopes down and labor supply \(w = \bar{a}_s + \bar{b}_s L\) slopes up. They cross at \((L^*, w^*)\). If the population is a fixed number \(N\), the model also gives the employment-population ratio \(L^*/N\). When you move a slider, the starting curves stay on the chart as dashed gray lines, so you can see the shift.

def labor_market(a_d=100.0, b_d=1.0, a_s=10.0, b_s=1.0):
    """Figure 7.3: labor supply, labor demand and the equilibrium (L*, w*)."""
    L_star, w_star = equilibrium(a_d, b_d, a_s, b_s)
    fig = go.Figure()
    if (a_d, b_d, a_s, b_s) != (100.0, 1.0, 10.0, 1.0):          # keep the starting curves for comparison
        add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid), "Starting curves", GRAY, "dash")
        add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid), "", GRAY, "dash")
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid, a_s, b_s), "Labor supply, Lˢ", TEAL)
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid, a_d, b_d), "Labor demand, Lᵈ", BLUE)
    add_point(fig, L_star, w_star, "")
    fig.update_layout(title=f"The labor market clears at w* = {w_star:.1f} and L* = {L_star:.1f}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Employment, L", range=[0, 100]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Wage, w", range=[0, 110]))
    return fig


Python note. interact calls the function and redraws its figure every time you move a slider. A FloatSlider chooses a number between min and max in steps of step, starting at value. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.


interact(labor_market,
         a_d=FloatSlider(value=100, min=80, max=120, step=5, description="demand intercept a_d", style=WIDE),
         b_d=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.75, max=1.5, step=0.25, description="demand slope b_d", style=WIDE),
         a_s=FloatSlider(value=10, min=0, max=30, step=5, description="supply intercept a_s", style=WIDE),
         b_s=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.75, max=1.5, step=0.25, description="supply slope b_s", style=WIDE));



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Figure 3 with a precomputed slider for the demand intercept
slider_figure(labor_market, "a_d", [80, 90, 100, 110, 120], start=100, label="demand intercept a_d")





                                
                                            




What to notice.

With our illustrative numbers the market clears at \(L^* = 45\) and \(w^* = 55\).
A higher \(\bar{a}_d\) (firms value every worker more) shifts demand up: the wage and employment rise.
A higher \(\bar{a}_s\) (people need a higher wage before they work) shifts supply up: the wage rises but employment falls.
Steeper curves (larger slopes) make employment respond less to a given shift.

Your turn. Raise the demand intercept \(\bar{a}_d\) from 100 to 110. By how much do \(L^*\) and \(w^*\) change? Check your answer with equilibrium(a_d=110).


Hint

With both slopes equal to 1, \(L^* = (\bar{a}_d - \bar{a}_s)/2\), so each extra unit of \(\bar{a}_d\) adds half a unit to \(L^*\).

title: Chapter 7: The Labor Market, Wages, and Unemployment
section: Figure 4: An income tax at rate τ
text:
Figure 4: An income tax at rate τ
Goal. See how a tax on labor income lowers employment and drives a wedge between the wage firms pay and the wage workers keep.
With a tax at rate \(\tau\), a worker keeps only \((1-\tau)w\) of the wage \(w\) the firm pays. To supply the same amount of work as before, workers now need a higher wage from the firm, \(w = (\bar{a}_s + \bar{b}_s L)/(1-\tau)\). Drawn against the wage firms pay, labor supply shifts back (up and to the left). The economy moves from \(A\) to \(B\).

def income_tax(tau=0.25, b_s=1.0):
    """Figure 7.4: a labor income tax tau shifts labor supply back; the economy moves from A to B."""
    L_A, w_A = equilibrium(b_s=b_s)
    L_B, w_B = equilibrium(b_s=b_s, tau=tau)
    kept = (1 - tau) * w_B                                       # what workers keep at B
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid, b_s=b_s), "Labor supply, no tax", GRAY, "dash")
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid, b_s=b_s) / (1 - tau), "Labor supply with the tax, Lˢ′", TEAL)
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid), "Labor demand, Lᵈ", BLUE)
    add_point(fig, L_A, w_A, "A")
    add_point(fig, L_B, w_B, "B")
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[L_B, L_B], y=[kept, w_B], mode="lines+markers", name="Tax wedge",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=6)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"τ = {tau:.0%}: L′ = {L_B:.1f}, firms pay w′ = {w_B:.1f}, workers keep {kept:.1f}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Employment, L", range=[0, 100]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Wage paid by firms, w", range=[0, 110]))
    return fig


interact(income_tax,
         tau=FloatSlider(value=0.25, min=0, max=0.5, step=0.05, description="tax rate τ", style=WIDE),
         b_s=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="supply slope b_s", style=WIDE));



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Figure 4 with a precomputed slider for the tax rate
slider_figure(income_tax, "tau", [0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5], start=0.25, label="tax rate τ")





                                
                                            




What to notice.

With a 25 percent tax, employment falls from 45 to about 37.1. Firms pay more (62.9 instead of 55), but workers keep less (47.1). The green bar is the tax per unit of work.
The textbook draws the taxed supply curve parallel to the old one. With a tax proportional to the wage, the new curve is a little steeper: the tax takes more when the wage is higher.
A flatter supply curve (smaller \(\bar{b}_s\)) means people respond more to the wage they keep, so the same tax cuts employment by more.

Your turn. What tax rate cuts employment from 45 to 30? Find it with the slider, then check it with equilibrium(tau=...).


Hint

Solve \(((1-\tau)\cdot 100 - 10)/((1-\tau) + 1) = 30\) for \((1-\tau)\), or try values of tau in steps of 0.05.

title: Chapter 7: The Labor Market, Wages, and Unemployment
section: Figure 5: A reduction in labor demand
text:
Figure 5: A reduction in labor demand
Goal. See what happens to the wage and employment when firms want fewer workers.
New rules that make firing workers costly, or a jump in the price of an input such as oil, can make firms less willing to hire. In the diagram, labor demand shifts down by an amount we call shift: \(w = (\bar{a}_d - \text{shift}) - \bar{b}_d L\). The economy moves from \(A\) to \(B\).

Python note. fig.add_annotation(...) with showarrow=True draws an arrow from the point (ax, ay) to the point (x, y). With axref="x" and ayref="y", both points are given in the units of the axes.


def demand_fall(shift=20.0, b_s=1.0):
    """Figure 7.5: labor demand shifts back by shift; the wage and employment both fall (A -> B)."""
    L_A, w_A = equilibrium(b_s=b_s)
    L_B, w_B = equilibrium(a_d=100 - shift, b_s=b_s)
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid), "Labor demand before, Lᵈ", GRAY, "dash")
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid, 100 - shift), "Labor demand after, Lᵈ′", BLUE)
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid, b_s=b_s), "Labor supply, Lˢ", TEAL)
    add_point(fig, L_A, w_A, "A")
    add_point(fig, L_B, w_B, "B")
    if shift > 0:
        fig.add_annotation(x=75, y=labor_demand(75, 100 - shift) + 1, ax=75, ay=labor_demand(75) - 1,
                           xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y", text="", showarrow=True,
                           arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor="black")
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Demand falls by {shift:.0f}: w {w_A:.1f} → {w_B:.1f}, L {L_A:.1f} → {L_B:.1f}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Employment, L", range=[0, 100]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Wage, w", range=[0, 110]))
    return fig

         shift=FloatSlider(value=20, min=0, max=40, step=5, description="fall in labor demand", style=WIDE),

text:
Figure 6: A reduction in labor demand with wage rigidity
Goal. See why a wage that does not fall turns a fall in demand into a much larger fall in employment.
Suppose the wage stays at its old level \(\bar{w} = w^*\) after labor demand falls. Firms then hire only what they want at \(\bar{w}\), so employment moves along the new demand curve to \(C\):
\[L'' = \frac{(\bar{a}_d - \text{shift}) - \bar{w}}{\bar{b}_d}\]
At \(\bar{w}\), the number of people who want to work is still \(L^*\), so \(L^* - L''\) people would like a job but cannot find one. Choose rigid or flexible with the buttons to compare \(C\) with \(B\).

def wage_rigidity(shift=20.0, wage="rigid"):
    """Figure 7.6: labor demand falls; with a rigid wage w-bar the economy moves to C instead of B."""
    L_A, w_bar = equilibrium()                                    # A: the old equilibrium sets w-bar
    L_B, w_B = equilibrium(a_d=100 - shift)                      # B: the wage is flexible
    L_C = demand_at_wage(w_bar, a_d=100 - shift)                 # C: firms' demand at w-bar
    jobless = supply_at_wage(w_bar) - L_C                        # want to work at w-bar, but no job
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid), "Labor demand before, Lᵈ", GRAY, "dash")
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid, 100 - shift), "Labor demand after, Lᵈ′", BLUE)
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid), "Labor supply, Lˢ", TEAL)
    add_point(fig, L_A, w_bar, "A")
    if wage == "rigid":
        add_point(fig, L_C, w_bar, "C")
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[L_C, L_A], y=[w_bar, w_bar], mode="lines", name="Want a job, cannot find one",
                                 line=dict(color=GREEN, width=6)))
        title = f"Rigid wage w̄ = {w_bar:.0f}: L″ = {L_C:.1f} (flexible: L′ = {L_B:.1f}); jobless gap {jobless:.1f}"
    else:
        add_point(fig, L_B, w_B, "B")
        title = f"Flexible wage: the wage falls to w′ = {w_B:.1f} and employment to L′ = {L_B:.1f}"
    fig.update_layout(title=title, xaxis=dict(title="Employment, L", range=[0, 100]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Wage, w", range=[0, 110]))
    return fig

What to notice.

With a flexible wage, a fall in demand of 20 moves the economy to \(B\): employment 35. With the wage stuck at \(\bar{w} = 55\) it moves to \(C\): employment 25, twice the fall.
At \(C\), 45 people want to work at the going wage but only 25 are hired: a gap of 20. Wage rigidity creates unemployment that a flexible wage would not.
This is the reason Keynes gave for the mass unemployment of the Great Depression, and rigid wages return in the short-run chapters of the book.


The bathtub model of unemployment
The textbook’s Section 7.4 explains the natural rate of unemployment with a simple model. The labor force \(\bar{L}\) is fixed, and each month a share \(\bar{s}\) of the employed lose their job (the job separation rate) while a share \(\bar{f}\) of the unemployed find one (the job finding rate):
\[E_t + U_t = \bar{L} \qquad (7.2) \qquad\qquad \Delta U_{t+1} = \bar{s}E_t - \bar{f}U_t \qquad (7.3)\]
Unemployment is like water in a bathtub: job losses are the faucet and job findings the drain. The level stops changing when the two flows are equal, which gives the steady-state rate
\[u^* = \frac{\bar{s}}{\bar{f} + \bar{s}} \qquad (7.4)\]

Python note. range(61) counts 0, 1, …, 60, one step per month. Each pass of the loop stores the current rate with .append and then applies equations (7.2) and (7.3) once. interact_manual adds a button, so nothing happens until you press it.


def bathtub_path(s=0.01, f=0.20):
    """Section 7.4: simulate the bathtub model for 60 months, starting at 10% unemployment."""
    L_bar, U = 100.0, 10.0                     # labor force and unemployed (only the ratio matters)
    months, rates = [], []
    for t in range(61):
        months.append(t)
        rates.append(100 * U / L_bar)
        E = L_bar - U                          # equation (7.2)
        U = U + s * E - f * U                  # equation (7.3)
    u_star = 100 * s / (f + s)                 # equation (7.4)
    path = pd.DataFrame({"month": months, "rate": rates})
    fig = px.line(path, x="month", y="rate", hover_name="month",
                  labels={"month": "Months from the start", "rate": "Unemployment rate (percent)"},
                  title=f"s = {s:.3f}, f = {f:.2f}: unemployment settles at u* = s/(f+s) = {u_star:.1f}%")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3))
    fig.add_hline(y=u_star, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 25])
    return fig

Key numbers: present discounted value
To value a college degree we need a tool from the textbook’s Section 7.6. A payment received \(T\) years from now is worth less than the same payment today, because money today can earn interest at rate \(R\). Its present discounted value is
\[pdv = \frac{\text{future value}}{(1 + R)^T} \qquad (7.7)\]
For a payment that arrives every year for \(n\) years, starting today, we add up the present values of all the payments. The geometric-series formula gives the sum directly:
\[pdv = \text{payment} \times \frac{1 - \left(\frac{1}{1+R}\right)^n}{1 - \frac{1}{1+R}} \qquad (7.14)\]

Python note. The loop in pdv adds one discounted payment per year, so we can check the formula. ** is a power: (1 + R) ** t is \((1+R)^t\). 100_000 is simply 100000; Python ignores the underscore, which only makes large numbers easier to read. :,.0f prints a number with thousands separators and no decimals.


def pdv(payment, R, years):
    """Equation (7.14): present value of `payment` received every year for `years` years, starting today."""
    total = 0.0
    for t in range(years):                       # t = 0 is today, t = 1 next year, ...
        total = total + payment / (1 + R) ** t
    return total

text:
Figure 9: Understanding the rising return to education
Goal. See how the college wage can rise even though many more people go to college.
Figure 8 showed both more college graduates and a higher college premium. In a supply-and-demand diagram, more supply alone would lower the college wage. So demand for college graduates must have shifted out too, and by more than supply. Panel (a) is the market for high school graduates, which we keep unchanged. Panel (b) is the market for college graduates, with demand \(w = (90 + \text{shift}_d) - 0.4L\) and supply \(w = (30 - \text{shift}_s) + 0.6L\). Before the shifts, the college wage is 66 and the high school wage 55, a premium of 20 percent.
We draw the college market in a function of its own, because Figure 13 uses it again. The equilibrium before the shifts is marked \(*\) and the one after them \(**\).

def college_market(fig, shift_d, shift_s, row=None, col=None):
    """Figures 7.9b and 7.13: the college labor market before (*) and after (**) both curves shift."""
    L_1, w_1 = equilibrium(a_d=90.0, b_d=0.4, a_s=30.0, b_s=0.6)
    L_2, w_2 = equilibrium(a_d=90.0 + shift_d, b_d=0.4, a_s=30.0 - shift_s, b_s=0.6)
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid, 30.0, 0.6), "Before the shifts", GRAY, "dash", row, col)
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid, 90.0, 0.4), "", GRAY, "dash", row, col)
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid, 30.0 - shift_s, 0.6), "Labor supply", TEAL, "solid", row, col)
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid, 90.0 + shift_d, 0.4), "Labor demand", BLUE, "solid", row, col)
    add_point(fig, L_1, w_1, "*", row, col)
    add_point(fig, L_2, w_2, "**", row, col)
    return w_1, w_2


Python note. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2) creates a figure with two panels side by side, and row=..., col=... tells each drawing function which panel to use.


def rising_return(shift_d=15.0, shift_s=10.0):
    """Figure 7.9: (a) the high school market is unchanged; (b) college demand shifts out more than supply."""
    L_hs, w_hs = equilibrium()
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) High school graduates", "(b) College graduates"))
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid), "", TEAL, "solid", 1, 1)
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid), "", BLUE, "solid", 1, 1)
    add_point(fig, L_hs, w_hs, "*", 1, 1)
    w_1, w_2 = college_market(fig, shift_d, shift_s, 1, 2)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Employment", range=[0, 100])
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Wage", range=[0, 110])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"College wage {w_1:.1f} → {w_2:.1f}; premium over high school "
                            f"{w_1 / w_hs - 1:.0%} → {w_2 / w_hs - 1:.0%}")
    return fig

title: Chapter 7: The Labor Market, Wages, and Unemployment
section: Summary
text:
Summary

The employment-population ratio rose for decades as women joined the labor force, while men’s ratio fell. Both the ratio and the unemployment rate swing sharply in recessions.
In the supply-and-demand model of the labor market, an income tax shifts supply back and lowers employment; a fall in labor demand lowers both the wage and employment. If the wage does not fall, employment falls even more and some people who want a job cannot find one.
The bathtub model gives the natural rate of unemployment, \(u^* = \bar{s}/(\bar{f} + \bar{s})\): about 5 percent with U.S. job finding and separation rates. Europe’s higher unemployment since the 1980s reflects adverse shocks combined with labor market institutions.
Present discounted values compare payments at different dates: a working life is worth millions of dollars today, and a college degree several hundred thousand.
The college premium rose while college graduates became more numerous, so demand for skills must have grown faster than supply. Inequality at the very top has risen sharply in the United States since 1980.
The next chapter turns to the other long-run topic of the book: inflation.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each model figure gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

section: The model in code
text:
The model in code
The chapter’s model is the quantity theory of money. Let \(M_t\) be the amount of money, \(V_t\) the velocity of money (how many times a year each dollar is used to buy goods), \(P_t\) the price level and \(Y_t\) real GDP. The theory has four equations (Table 8.3 of the textbook):







Equation
Meaning




\(M_t V_t = P_t Y_t\)
the quantity equation (8.1): money spent = nominal GDP


\(Y_t = \bar{Y}_t\)
real GDP comes from the growth model (the classical dichotomy)


\(V_t = \bar{V}\)
velocity is constant


\(M_t = \bar{M}_t\)
the central bank chooses the money supply



Only the price level is left for the quantity equation to pin down:
\[P_t^* = \frac{\bar{M}_t \bar{V}}{\bar{Y}_t} \qquad (8.2)\]
In growth rates, the growth of a product is the sum of the growth rates, so \(\bar{g}_M + \bar{g}_V = g_P + \bar{g}_Y\) (8.3). With constant velocity, \(\bar{g}_V = 0\), and inflation \(\pi = g_P\) is
\[\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y \qquad (8.4)\]
Inflation also links the two kinds of interest rates. The nominal rate \(i\) is paid in dollars, the real rate \(R\) in goods, and the Fisher equation says
\[i = R + \pi \qquad (8.5) \qquad\qquad R = i - \pi \qquad (8.6)\]

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing g_V=0.0 gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. All rates here are in percent.


def price_level(M, V, Y):
    """Equation (8.2): the price level that solves the quantity equation M V = P Y."""
    return M * V / Y


def qt_inflation(g_M, g_Y, g_V=0.0):
    """Equations (8.3)-(8.4): inflation = money growth + velocity growth - real GDP growth (percent)."""
    return g_M + g_V - g_Y


def nominal_rate(R, pi):
    """Equation (8.5), the Fisher equation: the nominal interest rate i = R + pi (percent)."""
    return R + pi


def real_rate(i, pi):
    """Equation (8.6): the real interest rate R = i - pi (percent)."""
    return i - pi

A quick check of the functions with the textbook’s examples.

Python note. An f-string such as f"V = {1000 / 200:.0f}" inserts a value into a piece of text; :.0f means “no decimals” and :.1f “one decimal”.


print(f"Nominal GDP 1,000 and money 200: velocity V = {1000 / 200:.0f}")
print(f"M = 200, V = 5, Y = 500:  price level P* = {price_level(200, 5, 500):.1f}")
print(f"Twice the money, M = 400: price level P* = {price_level(400, 5, 500):.1f}")
print(f"Money growth 7%, real GDP growth 4%:  inflation = {qt_inflation(7, 4):.0f}%")
print(f"Money growth 10%, real GDP growth 4%: inflation = {qt_inflation(10, 4):.0f}%")
print(f"Real rate 5%, inflation 3%: nominal rate i = {nominal_rate(5, 3):.0f}%")
machine_return = 5 + (100 * 1.03 - 100)         # output worth 5, plus the machine's price gain
print(f"A 100-dollar machine earns {machine_return:.0f} dollars: a nominal return of {machine_return / 100:.0%}")

M = 200, V = 5, Y = 500:  price level P* = 2.0
Twice the money, M = 400: price level P* = 4.0

Money growth 10%, real GDP growth 4%: inflation = 6%
Real rate 5%, inflation 3%: nominal rate i = 8%
A 100-dollar machine earns 8 dollars: a nominal return of 8%


Doubling the money supply doubles the price level and changes nothing real: this is the neutrality of money. And raising money growth from 7 to 10 percent raises inflation from 3 to 6 percent, one for one.
Equation (8.4) is a rule for growth rates, and it is exact only for small changes. To see how close it is, we let money and real GDP grow year by year and solve equation (8.2) in every year.

Python note. for t in range(years + 1) repeats the indented lines for t = 0, 1, …, years. rows.append([...]) adds one row to a list, and pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=[...]) turns the list into a table. .pct_change() gives the change from the previous row as a fraction.


def simulate_prices(g_M=7.0, g_Y=4.0, V=5.0, years=5):
    """Equation (8.2) year by year: money grows at g_M percent and real GDP at g_Y percent."""
    M, Y = 200.0, 500.0
    rows = []
    for t in range(years + 1):
        rows.append([t, M, Y, price_level(M, V, Y)])
        M = M * (1 + g_M / 100)
        Y = Y * (1 + g_Y / 100)
    path = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["year", "M", "Y", "P"])
    path["inflation"] = 100 * path.P.pct_change()
    return path

Python note. if ... else runs one block of code or the other. px.area draws a line and fills the area below it. With log_y=True the vertical axis is a ratio scale; tickvals chooses the numbers printed on it, and the range of a ratio axis is given in powers of 10 (np.log10(80)).


PRICE_TICKS = [100, 200, 400, 800, 1600]


def us_inflation(view="inflation rate"):
    """Figure 8.1: U.S. CPI inflation, or the price level it adds up to (1959 = 100, ratio scale)."""
    by_year = us.set_index("year").inflation_cpi
    if view == "inflation rate":
        fig = px.area(us, x="year", y="inflation_cpi", hover_name="year",
                      labels={"year": "Year", "inflation_cpi": "Inflation rate (percent)"},
                      title=f"U.S. inflation peaked at {by_year.max():.1f}% in {by_year.idxmax()} "
                            f"and reached {by_year[2022]:.1f}% in 2022")
        fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2))
        fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[-2, 15])
    else:
        factor = us.price_level.iloc[-1] / 100
        fig = px.line(us, x="year", y="price_level", log_y=True, hover_name="year",
                      labels={"year": "Year", "price_level": "Price level (1959 = 100, ratio scale)"},
                      title=f"Prices rose {factor:.1f}-fold from 1959 to {us.year.iloc[-1]}; steepest in the 1970s")
        fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3))
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=PRICE_TICKS, range=[np.log10(80), np.log10(1500)])
    return fig

The last row covers only 2020–2025, a decade that is not over yet. To choose other period lengths, we load the yearly M2 and CPI series behind the file and compute the growth rates ourselves.

Python note. range(1870, 2025, years) counts 1870, 1870 + years, … up to 2024: the first year of each period. min(a, b) is the smaller number, so the last period stops in 2025. x ** (1 / n) is the n-th root.


money = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "us_money_prices.csv").set_index("year")


def growth(x, start, end):
    """Average annual growth of x from start to end, in percent."""
    return 100 * ((x[end] / x[start]) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1)


def periods(years=10):
    """Figure 8.3: average money growth and inflation in periods of `years` years since 1870."""
    rows = []
    for start in range(1870, 2025, years):
        end = min(start + years, 2025)
        if years == 10 and end - start == 10:
            label = f"{start}s"
        else:
            label = f"{start}–{end}"
        kind = "full period" if end - start == years else "unfinished period"
        rows.append([label, start, end, growth(money.m2, start, end), growth(money.cpi, start, end), kind])
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["period", "start", "end", "money_growth", "inflation", "kind"])


check = periods(10)
print(f"Largest difference from fig8-3.csv: {(check.money_growth - decades.money_growth).abs().max():.3f} (money), "
      f"{(check.inflation - decades.inflation).abs().max():.3f} (inflation)")

Largest difference from fig8-3.csv: 0.000 (money), 0.000 (inflation)


The quantity theory says \(\pi = g_M + g_V - g_Y\). If velocity were constant and real GDP did not grow, every point would lie on the 45-degree line \(\pi = g_M\). Real GDP does grow, so points should lie below that line, by about \(g_Y - g_V\). The chart draws both lines; the lower one is shifted down by the average gap in the data.

Python note. px.scatter(..., symbol="kind") gives each kind of point its own marker, and symbol_map chooses the markers: full circles for full periods, an open circle for the unfinished one. .corr() is the correlation of two columns: 1 for points on a rising straight line, 0 for no relation.


KEY_DECADES = ["1870s", "1930s", "1940s", "1970s", "1980s", "2010s", "2020–2025"]


def money_and_prices(years=10):
    """Figure 8.3: U.S. money growth against inflation, one point per period of `years` years."""
    table = periods(years)
    gap = (table.money_growth - table.inflation).mean()
    r = table.money_growth.corr(table.inflation)
    labels = table.period.where(table.period.isin(KEY_DECADES) | (years == 20), "")   # hover shows the rest
    fig = px.scatter(table, x="money_growth", y="inflation", symbol="kind", text=labels, hover_name="period",
                     symbol_map={"full period": "circle", "unfinished period": "circle-open"},
                     labels={"money_growth": "Money growth (percent per year)", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent per year)",
                             "kind": ""},
                     title=f"{years}-year periods: correlation {r:.2f}, average gap g_M − π = {gap:.1f} points")
    fig.update_traces(marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=11), textposition="top center", textfont=dict(color=BLUE, size=11))
    g_M = np.array([-3, 18])
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=g_M, y=g_M, mode="lines", name="π = g_M (45-degree line)",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dot")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=g_M, y=qt_inflation(g_M, gap), mode="lines", name=f"π = g_M − {gap:.1f}",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY, line_width=1)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[-3, 18])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-5, 17])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.15, yanchor="top"))
    return fig

What to notice.

With decades, as in the textbook, the 1910s and the 1970s have the fastest inflation and fast money growth. The 1920s and 1930s had slow money growth and deflation: prices fell.
The points rise from left to right, roughly parallel to the 45-degree line, and about 4 points below it. The quantity theory says this gap is the growth of real GDP minus the growth of velocity.
With 5-year periods the cloud is wider. Wars and the Great Depression move prices a lot over a few years, and the theory is about the long run. Hover over the points to see the periods.

def world_money(g_Y=3.0, period="1990–2025"):
    """Figure 8.4: average money growth and inflation by economy, with the line pi = g_M - g_Y."""
    suffix = period.replace("–", "_")
    x, y, n_m, n_p = "money_growth_" + suffix, "inflation_" + suffix, "n_money_" + suffix, "n_infl_" + suffix
    above = (world[y] > qt_inflation(world[x], g_Y)).sum()
    fig = px.scatter(world, x=x, y=y, text="label", hover_name="country", log_x=True, log_y=True,
                     hover_data=[n_m, n_p],                       # years behind each average, shown on hover
                     labels={x: f"Money growth, {period} average (percent, ratio scale)",
                             y: "Inflation rate (percent, ratio scale)",
                             n_m: "years of money data", n_p: "years of inflation data"},
                     title=f"π = g_M − g_Y with g_Y = {g_Y:.0f}%: {above} of {len(world)} economies lie above the line")
    fig.update_traces(marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=8), textposition=list(world.position), textfont=dict(color=BLUE, size=11))
    g_M = np.geomspace(g_Y + 0.4, 900, 200)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=g_M, y=qt_inflation(g_M, g_Y), mode="lines", name=f"Quantity theory, π = g_M − {g_Y:.0f}",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=MONEY_TICKS, range=[np.log10(1.5), np.log10(900)])
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=INFLATION_TICKS, range=[np.log10(0.3), np.log10(4000)])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.02, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom"))
    return fig

The inflation tax
Why would a government let money grow so fast? Because printing money is one way to pay its bills. The government budget constraint says that spending \(G\) is paid with taxes \(T\), new borrowing \(\Delta B\), or new money \(\Delta M\):
\[G = T + \Delta B + \Delta M \qquad (8.7)\]
The revenue from new money is called seignorage, or the inflation tax. It is paid by everyone who holds money: when the price level doubles, a 200-dollar bill buys only what 100 dollars bought before.

def money_printed(G, T, dB):
    """Equation (8.7): the new money the government must issue, Delta M = G - T - Delta B."""
    return G - T - dB

title: Chapter 8: Inflation
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Inflation is the growth rate of the price level. U.S. inflation peaked at 13.5 percent in 1980, stayed near 2 percent for two decades, and jumped to 8 percent in 2022. A price index turns past prices into today’s dollars.
The quantity theory of money gives \(P^* = \bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}\) and \(\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y\): in the long run, faster money growth means higher inflation, one for one. U.S. decades and 165 economies line up as predicted, although velocity is not really constant.
The Fisher equation \(i = R + \pi\) turns nominal interest rates into real ones. U.S. real rates were negative in the 1970s and in most years since 2008.
Hyperinflations happen when governments cannot pay their bills with taxes or borrowing and print money instead: persistent high inflation is a fiscal problem. They can end as quickly as they start.
The next chapter starts the short-run part of the book, with an introduction to economic fluctuations.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

title: Chapter 9: An Introduction to the Short Run
section: The model in code
text:
The model in code
The short-run model takes the long run as given. Potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\) and the long-run inflation rate \(\bar{\pi}\) come from the long-run model, so they carry bars: they are exogenous here. The model explains how actual output \(Y_t\) and inflation \(\pi_t\) move around them.
Actual output is the long-run trend plus short-run fluctuations (equation 9.1). We measure the fluctuations in percent of potential output and call them short-run output:
\[\tilde{Y}_t \equiv \frac{Y_t - \bar{Y}_t}{\bar{Y}_t} \qquad (9.2)\]
When the economy booms, \(Y_t > \bar{Y}_t\) and \(\tilde{Y}_t > 0\). In a recession, \(\tilde{Y}_t < 0\). Two more relationships complete this first look at the short run:

the Phillips curve: inflation rises when output is above potential and falls when it is below, \(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t\). Chapter 12 calls the slope \(\bar{\nu}\) (the Greek letter nu);
Okun’s law: unemployment is above its natural rate \(\bar{u}\) when output is below potential, \(u_t - \bar{u} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\,\tilde{Y}_t\) (equation 9.3).

In the code, \(\tilde{Y}\), \(\Delta\pi\) and \(u-\bar{u}\) are all measured in percent (or percentage points), as in the textbook’s figures.
One baseline for every diagram. The textbook’s diagrams 9.1 and 9.6 print no numbers, so all the model figures of this notebook share one illustrative baseline:

potential output starts at \(\bar{Y}_0 = 100\) and grows by \(\bar{g} = 2\) percent a year;
short-run output swings between \(+2\) and \(-2\) percent (the \(\pm 2\%\) marked in Figure 9.1), in a cycle that repeats every 8 years;
the slope of the Phillips curve is \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), the textbook’s “about 1/3” for the United States;
long-run inflation is \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent, and Okun’s slope is \(-1/2\).

Figure 9 is the worked answer to a textbook exercise, which gives its own numbers (\(\bar{\nu} = 1\), \(\tilde{Y} = +3\%\)), and we use those there.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing g=2.0 gives the argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. ** means “to the power of”, and np.sin is the sine function, which draws a smooth wave (np.pi is the number π).


def potential_output(t, g=2.0, Y0=100.0):
    """Potential output Ybar_t: a smooth trend that grows g percent a year, from Y0 in year 0."""
    return Y0 * (1 + g / 100) ** t


def actual_output(t, A=2.0, g=2.0, cycle=8):
    """Actual output Y_t: potential output times (1 + a wave of +-A percent that repeats every `cycle` years)."""
    return potential_output(t, g) * (1 + A / 100 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / cycle))


def short_run_output(Y, Ybar):
    """Short-run output in percent: 100 (Y - Ybar) / Ybar   (equation 9.2)."""
    return 100 * (Y - Ybar) / Ybar


def phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu=0.33):
    """Change in inflation, percentage points: delta pi = nu * Y_tilde   (the Phillips curve, Figure 9.6)."""
    return nu * Y_tilde


def okun_law(Y_tilde, slope=-0.5):
    """Cyclical unemployment u - u_bar, percentage points: slope * Y_tilde   (Okun's law, equation 9.3)."""
    return slope * Y_tilde

Let us try the functions on the textbook’s own examples.

Python note. An f-string such as f"Y~ = {value:+.2f}%" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.2f means “show two decimals” and the + adds a sign.


print(f"Actual 980, potential 1,000:  Y~ = {short_run_output(980, 1000):+.2f}%")
print(f"Output 3% above potential:    delta pi = {phillips_curve(3.0):+.2f} points (slope 0.33)")
print(f"Output 6% below potential:    u - u_bar = {okun_law(-6.0):+.2f} points (Okun's law)")
print(f"Baseline in year 2: potential {potential_output(2):.2f}, actual {actual_output(2):.2f}, "
      f"Y~ = {short_run_output(actual_output(2), potential_output(2)):+.2f}%")

Actual 980, potential 1,000:  Y~ = -2.00%
Output 3% above potential:    delta pi = +0.99 points (slope 0.33)
Output 6% below potential:    u - u_bar = +3.00 points (Okun's law)
Baseline in year 2: potential 104.04, actual 106.12, Y~ = +2.00%


The first line is the textbook’s example: output of 980 against a potential of 1,000 is \(-20/1{,}000 = -2\) percent. With a slope of \(0.33\), output 3 percent above potential raises inflation by about 1 percentage point, and Okun’s law turns a 6 percent shortfall of output into unemployment 3 points above its natural rate.

section: Figure 1: Economic fluctuations and short-run output
text:
Figure 1: Economic fluctuations and short-run output
Goal. See how removing the trend from actual output leaves the ups and downs of the business cycle.
Panel (a) draws actual output \(Y_t\) around a smooth potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\). Panel (b) draws short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t\) from equation (9.2): the same wiggle, with the trend taken out. The gray bars in panel (a) are the gaps \(Y - \bar{Y}\) at the top of the boom and at the bottom of the slump.

Python note. np.linspace(0, 8, 200) creates 200 evenly spaced numbers from 0 to 8: the years at which we draw the curves. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2) makes a figure with two panels, and row=..., col=... tells add_trace where to draw. We fix the axis ranges so that you can see the curves move when a parameter changes.


def fluctuations(A=2.0, g=2.0):
    """Figure 9.1: actual and potential output (a) and short-run output (b), over one 8-year cycle."""
    t = np.linspace(0, 8, 200)                          # time, in years
    Y, Ybar = actual_output(t, A, g), potential_output(t, g)
    t_gap = np.array([2.0, 6.0])                        # the top of the boom and the bottom of the slump
    Y_gap, Ybar_gap = actual_output(t_gap, A, g), potential_output(t_gap, g)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) Actual and potential output",
                                                        "(b) Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Y, name="Actual output, Y", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Ybar, name="Potential output, Ȳ", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")),
                  row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[2, 2, None, 6, 6], y=[Ybar_gap[0], Y_gap[0], None, Ybar_gap[1], Y_gap[1]],
                             name="Gap, Y − Ȳ", mode="lines", line=dict(color=GRAY, width=4)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=short_run_output(Y, Ybar), name="Short-run output, Ỹ",
                             line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)), row=1, col=2)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, 8], y=[0, 0], name="Ỹ = 0: output at potential", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=2, dash="dash")), row=1, col=2)
    fig.add_annotation(x=2, y=A, xref="x2", yref="y2", text="Boom: Ỹ > 0", showarrow=False, yshift=14)
    fig.add_annotation(x=6, y=-A, xref="x2", yref="y2", text="Slump: Ỹ < 0", showarrow=False, yshift=-14)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Time (years)", range=[0, 8])
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Output", range=[94, 145], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-5.2, 5.2], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Boom: Ỹ = +{A:.1f}%   Slump: Ỹ = −{A:.1f}%   |   potential grows {g:.1f}% a year",
                      legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.2, yanchor="top"))
    return fig

Now the interactive version. Move the sliders and compare the two panels.

Python note. interact turns each argument of a function into a slider and calls the function again every time you move one. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.

         A=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.5, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="size of the swings A (%)", style=WIDE),
         g=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="growth of potential g (% a year)",
                       style=WIDE));



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Figure 1 with a precomputed slider for the growth of potential output
fig = slider_figure(fluctuations, "g", [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], start=2.0, label="growth of potential g (% a year)")
fig.update_layout(height=600)
fig.layout.sliders[0].pad.t = 140                              # put the slider below the legend
fig





                                
                                            




What to notice.

Panel (b) looks just like actual output in panel (a), without the upward trend. That is why economists also call \(\tilde{Y}\) detrended output.
Raise the growth of potential output to 4 percent. In panel (a) the slump almost disappears: actual output keeps rising and only grows more slowly. In panel (b) nothing changes. Strong growth hides the cycle, which is exactly what happens with real GDP in Figure 2.
Set \(\bar{g} = 0\) and the two panels look the same: potential output is then a constant 100, so \(Y - \bar{Y}\) and \(\tilde{Y}\) are the same numbers.

section: Figure 2: U.S. real GDP, actual and potential
text:
Figure 2: U.S. real GDP, actual and potential
Goal. Look at actual and potential GDP in the United States since 1929.
The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates U.S. potential output from 1949 on, with a version of the Solow model. Our data file adds an estimate for 1929–1948, a very smooth trend through actual GDP.

The Great Depression shows up clearly: output was 23 percent below potential in 1933. During World War II it was 35 percent above potential in 1944. But look at the first row: output 25 percent above potential in 1929. That is not a real boom. Nobody published potential output for those years, so the early values are only an estimate. Python note. rename(columns={...}) gives the columns readable names for the legend. px.line with a list y=[...] draws one line per column. log_y=True gives a ratio scale, tickvals sets the numbers printed on the axis, and on a ratio scale the axis range is given in powers of ten: np.log10(0.9).

def gdp_chart(scale="ratio"):
    """Figure 9.2: U.S. real GDP, actual and potential, 1929-2025 (trillions of 2022 dollars)."""
    fig = px.line(named, x="year", y=["Actual GDP", "Potential GDP"], log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
                  color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Trillions of 2022 dollars", "variable": "Series"},
                  title="Actual and potential GDP move together, except in the 1930s and 1940s")
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Potential GDP"), line_dash="dash")
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Actual GDP"), line_width=3)
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=TICKS, range=[np.log10(0.9), np.log10(32)])
    else:

    return fig

Potential output grows more slowly after the Great Recession of 2007–09 (see the key numbers below). The CBO builds potential output with a Solow-type model, so weak investment after 2008 meant less capital and slower potential growth.


Key numbers: the Depression, the war and slower potential growth

Python note. set_index("year") labels the rows by year, so potential[2007] is the value for 2007. .loc[1930:1939] keeps the rows from 1930 to 1939, and .mean() averages them.


by_year = gdp.set_index("year")
potential = by_year.gdp_potential


def potential_growth(start, end):
    """Average annual growth of potential output from year start to year end, in percent."""
    return 100 * ((potential[end] / potential[start]) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1)

print(f"Potential growth 1990-2007:         {potential_growth(1990, 2007):.1f}% a year")
print(f"Potential growth 2007-2019:         {potential_growth(2007, 2019):.1f}% a year")

Key numbers: what does a recession cost?
The textbook adds up the output lost in a slump: about 6 percent of a year’s GDP in a typical recession. We can measure it. We walk through the quarters, and each time \(\tilde{Y}\) turns negative we start adding up the shortfall until output is back at potential. A quarter is a quarter of a year, so each quarter adds \(-\tilde{Y}/4\) percent of a year’s GDP.

Python note. series.short_run_output.items() hands over one (date, value) pair at a time. None means “no value yet”: start is None is true while we are not inside a slump. total += x is short for total = total + x.


slumps = []
start, total = None, 0.0
for date, value in series.short_run_output.items():
    if value < 0:
        if start is None:                      # a new slump begins
            start, total = date, 0.0
        total += -value / 4                    # lost output, percent of a year's GDP
    elif start is not None:                    # output is back at potential: the slump is over
        years = (date - start).days / 365.25
        slumps.append([start.strftime("%Y-%m"), date.strftime("%Y-%m"), years, total])
        start = None
slumps = pd.DataFrame(slumps, columns=["Slump starts", "Back at potential", "Years", "Lost output (% of GDP)"])

text:
Figure 6: The Phillips curve
Goal. Draw the Phillips curve and see how short-run output moves inflation.
Think of a hot holiday toy. When demand is high, the firm that makes it runs overtime and pays its workers more, and the toy is scarce. So its price rises faster than usual. In a booming economy, it is as if every firm made the hot toy: all of them raise prices faster than the current inflation rate, so inflation goes up. In a slump the opposite happens. The Phillips curve puts this in one line:
\[\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t\]
When output is at potential (\(\tilde{Y} = 0\)), inflation is steady. Our function phillips_curve from “The model in code” draws the line. The black dot is the economy, at the short-run output you choose.

Python note. fig.add_shape(type="line", ...) draws a straight segment, here the dashed guides from the dot to the axes. An if ... elif ... else block picks one of three cases.


def phillips_diagram(nu=0.33, Y_tilde=0.0):
    """Figure 9.6: the Phillips curve delta pi = nu * Y_tilde, with the economy at Y_tilde."""
    Y = np.linspace(-6, 6, 100)
    dpi = phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu)
    if dpi > 0:
        verdict = "inflation rises"
    elif dpi < 0:
        verdict = "inflation falls"
    else:
        verdict = "inflation is steady"
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Y, y=phillips_curve(Y, nu), name="Phillips curve", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[Y_tilde], y=[dpi], name="The economy", mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=13)))
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=Y_tilde, y0=-3.2, x1=Y_tilde, y1=dpi, line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash"))
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=-6.5, y0=dpi, x1=Y_tilde, y1=dpi, line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=-3.2, y=2.8, text="← Slumping economy (Ỹ < 0)", showarrow=False)
    fig.add_annotation(x=3.2, y=-2.8, text="Booming economy (Ỹ > 0) →", showarrow=False)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Ỹ = {Y_tilde:+.2f}%  →  Δπ = {nu:.2f} × ({Y_tilde:+.2f}) = {dpi:+.2f} points: {verdict}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)", range=[-6.5, 6.5], zeroline=True),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Change in inflation, Δπ (points)", range=[-3.2, 3.2], zeroline=True))
    return fig


interact(phillips_diagram,
         nu=FloatSlider(value=0.33, min=0.05, max=1.0, step=0.01, description="slope ν", style=WIDE),
         Y_tilde=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-5.0, max=5.0, step=0.5, description="short-run output Ỹ (%)", style=WIDE));



Show the code of the website version

What to notice.

To the right of zero (a boom), \(\Delta\pi > 0\): inflation rises. To the left (a slump), \(\Delta\pi < 0\): inflation falls.
The line always goes through the origin: only output at potential keeps inflation steady.
A steeper curve (a larger \(\bar{\nu}\)) means a boom raises inflation faster, but also that a slump brings it down faster.


How the short-run model works: the Volcker disinflation
In 1979 U.S. inflation was above 11 percent (Figure 5), and the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker set out to bring it down. The Phillips curve says that the only way to lower inflation is to push output below potential. Tight monetary policy did exactly that: short-run output averaged about \(-6\) percent in 1982 (Figure 3 shows the quarters). The model then predicts falling inflation, and inflation did fall to about 3 percent by 1983.
Let us check the model’s prediction for 1981–1983 with the annual short-run output of Figure 7 below.

text:
Figure 9: The Phillips curve and the booming economy
Goal. Answer the textbook’s exercise “Overstimulating the economy”: what happens if policymakers keep output 3 percent above potential every year?
The economy starts at potential with inflation at its long-run rate, \(\bar{\pi} = 2\%\). Then output is held at \(\tilde{Y} = +3\%\). The Phillips curve says inflation rises by \(\Delta\pi = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) every year:
\[\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t\]
With the textbook’s slope \(\bar{\nu} = 1\), inflation goes from 2 to 5, 8 and 11 percent in three years. A computer can apply this equation year after year: a simulation.

Python note. A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each year. pi_path[-1] is the last number in the list, last year’s inflation, and pi_path.append(...) adds this year’s at the end. range(1, years + 1) counts 1, 2, …, years.


def simulate_inflation(pi_bar=2.0, nu=1.0, Y_tilde=3.0, years=5):
    """Inflation year by year when output is held at Y_tilde: pi_t = pi_(t-1) + nu * Y_tilde."""
    pi_path = [pi_bar]                                    # year 0: inflation at its long-run rate
    for year in range(1, years + 1):
        pi_path.append(pi_path[-1] + phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu))
    return np.arange(years + 1), np.array(pi_path)


years, pi_path = simulate_inflation()
print("Inflation, years 0 to 5:", pi_path)

Inflation, years 0 to 5: [ 2.  5.  8. 11. 14. 17.]


The figure has two panels: (a) the Phillips curve with the economy at potential and in the boom, and (b) the inflation path that the boom produces.

def booming_economy(pi_bar=2.0, nu=1.0, Y_tilde=3.0):
    """Figure 9.9: the economy held at Y_tilde on the Phillips curve (a) and the inflation path (b)."""
    years, pi_path = simulate_inflation(pi_bar, nu, Y_tilde)
    dpi = phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu)
    Y = np.linspace(-6.5, 6.5, 100)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) The Phillips curve", "(b) Inflation, year by year"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=Y, y=phillips_curve(Y, nu), name="Phillips curve", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4)),
                  row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, Y_tilde], y=[0, dpi], name="At potential and in the boom", mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=12)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=pi_path, name="Inflation, π", mode="lines+markers",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), marker=dict(size=9)), row=1, col=2)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, 5], y=[pi_bar, pi_bar], name="Long-run inflation, π̄", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")), row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)", range=[-6.5, 6.5], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Change in inflation, Δπ", range=[-6.5, 6.5], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Years of the boom", range=[-0.3, 5.3], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Inflation (percent)", range=[-25, 35], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Δπ = {nu:.2f} × ({Y_tilde:+.2f}) = {dpi:+.2f} a year: "
                            f"π = {pi_path[0]:.2f} → {pi_path[1]:.2f} → {pi_path[2]:.2f} → {pi_path[3]:.2f}%",
                      legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.2, yanchor="top"))
    return fig

What to notice.

Holding output above potential does not raise inflation once: it raises it every year. The cost of a permanent boom is ever-rising inflation.
The steeper the Phillips curve, the faster inflation climbs. With the U.S. slope of about 0.33, inflation rises by about 1 point a year instead of 3, slower but without end.
Set \(\tilde{Y}\) below zero and the same mechanism brings inflation down: that is how a recession fights inflation.

title: Chapter 9: An Introduction to the Short Run
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Actual output is potential output plus short-run fluctuations. Short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t = (Y_t - \bar{Y}_t)/\bar{Y}_t\) is positive in a boom and negative in a recession.
U.S. recessions push output a few percent below potential, cost millions of jobs and, in total, several percent of a year’s GDP. Potential output is only estimated, so the measured gaps change when the data are revised.
Inflation usually falls during a recession. The Phillips curve \(\Delta\pi = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) captures this, with a U.S. slope of about 1/3; oil and other shocks move inflation too.
Okun’s law links output and unemployment: each point of output below potential adds about half a point of unemployment.
The next chapter uses this short-run lens on the Great Recession and the Covid-19 pandemic.

# Libraries used in this chapter

    import google.colab

    pass                                        # not running in Colab: nothing to do

DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/ch10/"

The next cell defines a helper that only the book website needs. Run it and move on.


Show the helper code
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

title: Chapter 10: The Great Recession and the Covid-19 Pandemic: A First Look
section: The model in code
text:
The model in code
This chapter has no new economic model. It describes two recessions with data, and it adds a few tools from financial economics that later chapters use. We put the tools here once and reuse them.
Measuring a crash. Most figures ask the same question: how far did a series fall from its peak to its trough? The answer is a percent change,
\[\%\Delta = 100 \times \left(\frac{X_{\text{trough}}}{X_{\text{peak}}} - 1\right).\]

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. The text in triple quotes is a short description. For a pandas Series with dates as row labels, series[start:end] keeps the rows between two dates, .idxmax() gives the date of the largest value and .idxmin() the date of the smallest. A function can return several results at once, separated by commas.


def percent_change(new, old):
    """Percent change from old to new: 100 (new / old - 1)."""
    return 100 * (new / old - 1)


def peak_to_trough(series, start, end):
    """The highest point between start and end, the lowest point after it, and the fall in percent."""
    window = series[start:end]
    peak = window.idxmax()                      # date of the highest value
    trough = window[peak:].idxmin()             # date of the lowest value after the peak
    return peak, trough, percent_change(window[trough], window[peak])

Recessions. Five figures shade the U.S. recessions, as dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER). The file recessions.csv lists, for each recession since 1953, the peak (the last month before the recession) and the trough (its last month), and the same dates in quarters. One small function adds the shaded bands to any figure.

Python note. parse_dates=[...] turns text such as "2007-12-01" into real dates. A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each recession: zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough) hands over one (peak, trough) pair at a time. The if skips recessions that ended before the chart starts, and fig.add_vrect shades the band between two dates.


recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv",
                         parse_dates=["peak", "trough", "peak_quarter", "trough_quarter"])


def shade_recessions(fig, start="2000-01-01"):
    """Shade every NBER recession that ends after `start` (Figures 2, 3, 7, 8 and 9)."""
    for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
        if trough >= pd.Timestamp(start):
            fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    return fig

The Great Recession runs from the peak in December 2007 to the trough in June 2009, and the Covid-19 recession from February to April 2020, only two months.

Balance sheets and leverage (Table 10.3)
A balance sheet lists what an institution owns, its assets, and what it owes, its liabilities. The difference is its equity, or net worth: the value that belongs to its owners. Leverage is the ratio of liabilities to net worth:
\[\text{net worth} = \text{assets} - \text{liabilities}, \qquad \text{leverage} = \frac{\text{liabilities}}{\text{net worth}}.\]
The textbook’s hypothetical bank (Table 10.3, billions of dollars) is a small table.

Python note. pd.Series({...}) builds a list of numbers with labels from a dictionary, a set of key: value pairs in curly braces. .sum() adds up all the values.


def net_worth(assets, liabilities):
    """Equity (net worth) = total assets - total liabilities (Table 10.3)."""
    return assets - liabilities


def leverage(liabilities, equity):
    """Leverage ratio = total liabilities / net worth."""
    return liabilities / equity


assets = pd.Series({"Loans": 1000, "Investments": 900, "Cash and reserves": 100})
liabilities = pd.Series({"Deposits": 1000, "Short-term debt": 400, "Long-term debt": 400})
equity = net_worth(assets.sum(), liabilities.sum())
print(f"Total assets {assets.sum():,}, total liabilities {liabilities.sum():,}, net worth {equity:,}")
print(f"Leverage = {liabilities.sum():,} / {equity} = {leverage(liabilities.sum(), equity):.0f}")
print(f"Capital ratio = {100 * equity / assets.sum():.0f}% of assets; reserves = "
      f"{100 * assets['Cash and reserves'] / liabilities['Deposits']:.0f}% of deposits")

Total assets 2,000, total liabilities 1,800, net worth 200
Leverage = 1,800 / 200 = 9
Capital ratio = 10% of assets; reserves = 10% of deposits


With a leverage of 9, each 10 dollars of assets is financed by 9 dollars of debt and only 1 dollar of the owners’ money. Now let the investments gain or lose value. The liabilities do not change, so all of the gain or loss lands on net worth:

for new_investments in [1000, 600]:
    new_equity = net_worth(assets.sum() - assets["Investments"] + new_investments, liabilities.sum())
    print(f"Investments {assets['Investments']} -> {new_investments}: return "
          f"{percent_change(new_investments, assets['Investments']):+.1f}%, net worth {equity} -> {new_equity}, "
          f"return to the owners {percent_change(new_equity, equity):+.1f}%")

Investments 900 -> 1000: return +11.1%, net worth 200 -> 300, return to the owners +50.0%
Investments 900 -> 600: return -33.3%, net worth 200 -> -100, return to the owners -150.0%


A gain of 11 percent on the investments is a gain of 50 percent for the owners. A loss of a third of the investments, only 15 percent of all assets, turns net worth negative: the bank is insolvent. The same arithmetic works for a house bought for 500,000 dollars with 20 percent down:

house, mortgage = 500_000, 400_000
for price_change in [10, -10, -20]:
    new_equity = net_worth(house * (1 + price_change / 100), mortgage)
    print(f"House price {price_change:+d}%: equity {house - mortgage:,} -> {new_equity:,.0f} "
          f"({percent_change(new_equity, house - mortgage):+.0f}%)")

House price +10%: equity 100,000 -> 150,000 (+50%)
House price -10%: equity 100,000 -> 50,000 (-50%)
House price -20%: equity 100,000 -> 0 (-100%)


How small a fall wipes out the owners? Net worth is the share \(1/(1+\text{leverage})\) of assets, so a fall in asset values of that size leaves nothing. Bear Stearns had a leverage of about 35 when it collapsed in 2008:

for L in [9, 35]:
    print(f"Leverage {L}: assets need to fall by only {100 / (1 + L):.1f}% to wipe out net worth")

Leverage 9: assets need to fall by only 10.0% to wipe out net worth
Leverage 35: assets need to fall by only 2.8% to wipe out net worth


With a leverage of 35, a fall of less than 3 percent in the value of its assets was enough. The rest of the chapter shows how far house and stock prices actually fell.

Figure 1: A bursting bubble in U.S. housing prices?
Goal. Measure the boom and bust in U.S. house prices that started the financial crisis.
Robert Shiller’s index measures the price of a typical U.S. house, divided by the consumer price index so that it is in real terms, with 1953 = 100. We read it with dates as row labels, as a Series called house.

Python note. set_index("date") makes the dates the row labels, and .real_home_price_index then picks one column as a Series. .tail() shows the last five rows.


housing = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig10-1.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
house = housing.set_index("date").real_home_price_index
