# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

section: The model in code
text:
The model in code
The figures of this chapter are all data, and they all rest on a few lines of national income accounting. We write these accounting rules once, as small functions, and every figure reuses them. Then we use the same functions to solve the textbook’s three small trade examples (Tables 19.1 to 19.5).
The trade balance. Exports \(EX\) are goods and services that a country sells abroad, and imports \(IM\) are those it buys abroad. The trade balance, or net exports, is the difference, \(NX \equiv EX - IM\). A positive \(NX\) is a trade surplus, a negative one a trade deficit. Figures always show such flows as a share of GDP, \(100 \times X / Y\), so that years and countries of different size can be compared.
The national income identity. Everything an economy produces, \(Y\), is consumed (\(C\)), invested (\(I\)), bought by the government (\(G\)) or sold abroad on net (\(NX\)): \(Y = C + I + G + NX\). Solved for net exports,
\[NX = Y - (C + I + G), \qquad\text{so}\qquad NX < 0 \;\Rightarrow\; C + I + G > Y \quad (19.1)\]
and \(NX > 0 \Rightarrow C + I + G < Y\) (19.2). A country with a trade deficit uses more goods than it produces; the rest comes from abroad, on credit.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. The text in triple quotes is a short description. The same function works for single numbers and for whole columns of a data table, because pandas does arithmetic on every row at once.


def share_of_gdp(x, gdp):
    """Any variable as a percent of GDP: 100 x / Y."""
    return 100 * x / gdp


def net_exports(exports, imports):
    """The trade balance (net exports): NX = EX - IM."""
    return exports - imports


def net_exports_from_uses(Y, C, I, G):
    """The national income identity Y = C + I + G + NX solved for NX (equations 19.1 and 19.2)."""
    return Y - (C + I + G)

A quick check with round numbers: an economy produces 100, consumes 70, invests 20 and its government buys 15.

Y, C, I, G = 100, 70, 20, 15
NX = net_exports_from_uses(Y, C, I, G)
print(f"NX = {Y} - ({C} + {I} + {G}) = {NX}, or {share_of_gdp(NX, Y):.0f}% of GDP")
print(f"Domestic uses C + I + G = {C + I + G} > Y = {Y}: the country runs a trade deficit")

NX = 100 - (70 + 20 + 15) = -5, or -5% of GDP
Domestic uses C + I + G = 105 > Y = 100: the country runs a trade deficit



Trade balances from GDP shares
The Penn World Table, the source of Figures 3 and 4, does not report net exports directly. It reports the shares of GDP that go to consumption, investment and government purchases: \(c = C/Y\), \(i = I/Y\) and \(g = G/Y\). Dividing the identity by \(Y\) gives the trade balance as a share of GDP, \(NX/Y = 1 - c - i - g\). In code, this is the same identity with \(Y = 1\):

def trade_balance_share(c, i, g):
    """NX as a percent of GDP from the GDP shares of C, I and G: 100 (1 - c - i - g)."""
    return 100 * net_exports_from_uses(1, c, i, g)


def share_of_us_gdp(share, gdp, gdp_us):
    """Rescale a share of a country's own GDP to a share of U.S. GDP (Figure 19.3, second bar)."""
    return share * gdp / gdp_us


print(f"c = 0.55, i = 0.25, g = 0.18: trade balance {trade_balance_share(0.55, 0.25, 0.18):.1f}% of GDP")

c = 0.55, i = 0.25, g = 0.18: trade balance 2.0% of GDP




Saving, investment and the trade balance (equation 19.6)
Total saving pays for investment. Saving comes from three sources: households, \(Y - T - C\); the government, \(T - G\); and foreigners, \(IM - EX\), the goods they send us on credit. Domestic saving is \(S \equiv (Y - T - C) + (T - G) = Y - C - G\). Put into the identity, \(Y - C - G = I + NX\), that is
\[\underbrace{NX}_{\text{trade balance}} = \underbrace{S - I}_{\text{net capital outflow}}. \quad (19.6)\]
A country that invests more than it saves (\(S < I\)) must borrow the difference abroad, and it does so by running a trade deficit. Two more functions measure the data over time: an average over a window of years and the sum of past flows, which turns yearly trade balances into a stock of foreign assets or debt.

Python note. For a table whose rows are years, data.loc[start:end] keeps the rows from start to end, both included, and .mean() averages them (one average per column). .cumsum() is the cumulative sum: row by row, the sum of all values so far.


def domestic_saving(I, NX):
    """Domestic saving S = Y - C - G, from equation (19.6): S = I + NX."""
    return I + NX


def net_capital_outflow(S, I):
    """Equation (19.6): the trade balance equals domestic saving minus investment, NX = S - I."""
    return S - I


def period_average(data, start, end):
    """Simple average over the years start to end (rows are years): one number per column."""
    return data.loc[start:end].mean()


def accumulate(start_value, flows):
    """Net foreign assets: start from start_value and add each year's trade balance."""
    return start_value + flows.cumsum()


S = Y - C - G                                   # the economy of the quick check above
print(f"S = {S}, I = {I}: S - I = {net_capital_outflow(S, I)}, the same as NX = {NX}")
print(f"... and back again: S = I + NX = {domestic_saving(I, NX)}")

S = 15, I = 20: S - I = -5, the same as NX = -5

Trade across time (Table 19.1)
Two islands grow wheat, which cannot be stored. Oddtopia has a harvest of 100 bushels in odd years and nothing in even years; Eventopia has the opposite luck. Each island lends half of a good harvest to the other and is repaid the next year, so both eat 50 bushels every year. With no investment and no government, \(NX = Y - C\): the harvest minus what is eaten. The sum of past trade balances is what the other island owes.

Python note. pd.DataFrame({...}) builds a table from a dictionary of columns. The for loop repeats the indented lines for each island, and island + " harvest" glues two pieces of text into a column name. .T turns the table on its side, so that the years become columns, as in the textbook.

Each island runs a deficit in its bad years and a surplus in its good years, and both smooth their consumption perfectly: this is risk sharing. The average trade balance is zero: in the long run, trade must be balanced, because nobody lends without being repaid. A deficit today is a promise of a surplus later.


Comparative advantage: the North and the South (Tables 19.2 to 19.5)
Two countries consume two goods, apples and computers, and spend half of their income on each. Labor is the only input (Table 19.2). Prices are quoted in apples, so an apple costs 1, a computer costs \(p\) apples, and the wage \(w\) is in apples too. With half of income spent on each good, a worker eats \(w/2\) apples (19.3) and buys \(w/(2p)\) computers (19.4).

x_s, z_s, L_s = 100, 2, 400         # South

The North is better at both goods: it has an absolute advantage in both. But its lead is much larger in computers (8 times) than in apples (1.6 times), so it has a comparative advantage in computers, and the South in apples.
Autarky (no trade). A worker can make \(x\) apples or \(z\) computers, so the wage is \(w = x\) apples, and both sectors pay the same only if a computer costs \(p = x/z\) apples. Half of the workers make each good.

Python note. pd.Series({...}) builds a list of numbers with labels from a dictionary. pd.DataFrame then puts two such lists side by side as the columns “North” and “South”. pd.concat([...], axis=1, keys=[...]) places two tables next to each other under two headings.


def autarky(x, z, L):
    """Table 19.3: a closed economy whose L workers each make x apples or z computers."""
    w = x                        # the wage in apples: what a worker makes in the apple sector
    p = x / z                    # the price of a computer: both sectors must pay the same wage
    return pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w,
                      "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                      "Apples per person": w / 2,              # equation (19.3), an apple costs 1
                      "Computers per person": w / 2 / p,       # equation (19.4)
                      "Workers making apples (%)": 50,
                      "Workers making computers (%)": 50,
                      "Apples produced": L / 2 * x,
                      "Computers produced": L / 2 * z})

Free trade. Computers cost 10 apples in the North and 50 in the South, so it pays to buy computers in the North and sell them in the South (arbitrage). Each country then makes only the good it is relatively good at: the North makes only computers and the South only apples. World spending on computers equals world spending on apples (each is half of world income), so \(p \times \text{computers} = \text{apples}\), and the world price is \(p = \text{apples} / \text{computers}\).

def free_trade(x_n, z_n, L_n, x_s, z_s, L_s):
    """Table 19.4: the North makes only computers, the South only apples, and they trade."""
    computers = L_n * z_n                      # world production of computers
    apples = L_s * x_s                         # world production of apples
    p = apples / computers                     # half of world spending goes to each good
    w_n, w_s = z_n * p, x_s                    # wages in apples
    north = pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w_n, "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                       "Apples per person": w_n / 2, "Computers per person": w_n / 2 / p,
                       "Workers making apples (%)": 0, "Workers making computers (%)": 100,
                       "Apples produced": 0, "Computers produced": computers})
    south = pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w_s, "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                       "Apples per person": w_s / 2, "Computers per person": w_s / 2 / p,
                       "Workers making apples (%)": 100, "Workers making computers (%)": 0,
                       "Apples produced": apples, "Computers produced": 0})
    return pd.DataFrame({"North": north, "South": south})

In the 1950s exports and imports were each only about 4 to 5 percent of GDP. Since then exports have more than doubled and imports more than tripled.

The Oddtopia example says that the trade balance must average zero over a long period. The figure function shades a window of years and reports the average trade balance in it, using our period_average.

Python note. min(a, b) and max(a, b) give the smaller and the larger of two numbers, so the window stays valid even if the two sliders cross. (series < 0).sum() counts the years with a deficit, because each True counts as 1. add_vrect shades a band between two x values, and add_shape(type="line", ...) draws a segment.


def trade_balance_chart(start=1976, end=2025):
    """Figure 19.2: the U.S. trade balance (% of GDP), with its average from start to end."""
    start, end = min(start, end), max(start, end)         # in case the sliders cross
    avg = period_average(us.trade_balance, start, end)
    deficits = (us.trade_balance.loc[start:end] < 0).sum()
    fig = px.line(us.reset_index(), x="year", y="trade_balance", color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "trade_balance": "Percent of GDP"},
                  title=f"{start}–{end}: average trade balance {avg:+.2f}% of GDP, "
                        f"deficits in {deficits} of {end - start + 1} years")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=start, x1=end, y0=avg, y1=avg, line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3, dash="dot"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=1957, y=1.5, text="Trade surplus", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=14))
    fig.add_annotation(x=1962, y=-4.5, text="Trade deficit", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=14))
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1948, 2027])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-6.5, 2.5], tickvals=[-6, -5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2])
    return fig


Python note. interact turns each argument of the function into a widget and draws the figure again whenever you move one. IntSlider is a slider for whole numbers. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.

         end=IntSlider(value=2025, min=1950, max=2025, step=1, description="last year", style=WIDE));

The second bar of the textbook’s figure shows each country’s trade balance as a share of U.S. GDP, so the bars of different countries can be added up and compared with the U.S. deficit: we multiply the share of own GDP by the country’s GDP and divide by U.S. GDP.

def world_balance_chart(year=2023, vintage="PWT 11.0"):
    """Figure 19.3: the trade balance as a share of own GDP and of U.S. GDP, in one year."""
    if vintage == "PWT 10.01":
        year = min(year, 2019)                              # PWT 10.01 ends in 2019
    rows = pwt[(pwt.year == year) & (pwt.vintage == vintage) & pwt.country.isin(FIG3)]
    one = rows.set_index("country").loc[FIG3]
    bars = pd.DataFrame({"Share of own GDP": one.trade_balance,
                         "Share of U.S. GDP": share_of_us_gdp(one.trade_balance, one.cgdpo, one.loc["U.S.", "cgdpo"])})
    long = bars.reset_index().melt(id_vars="country", var_name="Measure", value_name="Percent")
    fig = px.bar(long, x="country", y="Percent", color="Measure", barmode="group", hover_name="country",
                 color_discrete_map={"Share of own GDP": BLUE, "Share of U.S. GDP": GREEN},
                 labels={"country": "", "Percent": "Percent"},
                 title=f"{year} ({vintage}): U.S. deficit {bars.loc['U.S.', 'Share of own GDP']:.1f}% of GDP; "
                       f"China's surplus {bars.loc['China', 'Share of U.S. GDP']:.1f}% of U.S. GDP")
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-9, 12.5], tickvals=[-8, -6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top", title=""))
    return fig

Figure 4: The trade balance in rapidly growing countries
Goal. Test whether fast-growing countries borrow from abroad, as consumption smoothing predicts.
A country that expects to be much richer tomorrow should borrow today, like a student who expects a high income later: it should run trade deficits. The textbook checks this for five fast-growing economies. Each bar is the simple average of the yearly trade balance over a window of years. We first make a table with one row per year and one column per country, so that period_average gives one average per country.

Python note. .pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="trade_balance") turns a long table into a wide one: years as rows, countries as columns. [FIG4] then keeps the columns in the textbook’s order. With text_auto=".1f", px.bar writes each bar’s value, with one decimal, on the bar.


FIG4 = ["China", "India", "Singapore", "Ireland", "S. Korea"]
fast = pwt[pwt.country.isin(FIG4)]


def fast_growers_chart(start=2000, end=2023, vintage="PWT 11.0"):
    """Figure 19.4: the average trade balance (% of own GDP) of five fast-growing economies."""
    wide = fast[fast.vintage == vintage].pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="trade_balance")[FIG4]
    end = min(end, wide.index.max())                         # PWT 10.01 ends in 2019
    avg = period_average(wide, start, end)
    bars = avg.rename("average").reset_index()
    fig = px.bar(bars, x="country", y="average", text_auto=".1f", hover_name="country",
                 color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN],
                 labels={"country": "", "average": "Percent of own GDP"},
                 title=f"{start}–{end} ({vintage}): {(avg > 0).sum()} of 5 fast-growing economies "
                       f"ran trade surpluses on average")
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-5, 30], tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30])
    return fig

title: Chapter 19: International Trade
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Trade has become much more important: U.S. exports and imports have risen from about 4 percent of GDP each in 1950 to 11 and 14 percent. Since 1976 imports have exceeded exports every year, and the trade deficit reached 5.7 percent of GDP in 2006.
The national income identity shows what a deficit means: with \(NX < 0\), a country uses more than it produces (\(C + I + G > Y\)), and it invests more than it saves (\(NX = S - I\)). The deficit is borrowing from the rest of the world, and the sum of past deficits is the net foreign debt, about 70 percent of U.S. GDP today.
Trade can make everyone better off: across time it shares risks (Oddtopia and Eventopia), and across goods it lets countries specialize by comparative advantage (the North and the South). Free migration follows absolute advantage and can raise world output even more.
The data hold surprises: fast-growing economies tend to run surpluses, not deficits, and the large U.S. budget deficits of the 1980s and 2000s came with large trade deficits (the twin deficits). They also teach care: the textbook’s “2019” bars are 2017 data, and revisions changed the recent foreign debt by up to 16 points of GDP.
The next chapter, exchange rates and international finance, brings trade into the short-run model and asks how the exchange rate adjusts.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

title: Chapter 20: Exchange Rates and International Finance
section: The model in code
text:
The model in code
Exchange rates in the long run. The nominal exchange rate \(E\) is the number of units of foreign currency that one dollar buys, for example 0.92 euros. The law of one price says that, in the long run, a good sells for the same price everywhere once prices are written in the same currency. With \(P\) the U.S. price and \(P^w\) the foreign (“world”) price,
\[EP = P^w. \qquad (20.1)\]
Apply it to the whole basket of goods of each economy. The quantity theory of money pins down the two price levels in the long run, so the law of one price pins down the exchange rate:
\[\bar{E} = \frac{\bar{P}^w}{\bar{P}}. \qquad (20.3)\]
The real exchange rate \(EP/P^w\) is the price of U.S. goods in units of foreign goods. If the law of one price holds, it equals 1 in the long run, \(\overline{RER} = \bar{E}P/\bar{P}^w = 1\) (20.4). In the short run, \(E\) jumps with financial news while prices are sticky, so the real exchange rate moves with \(E\).
Exchange rates in the short-run model. When the U.S. real interest rate \(R_t\) rises, investors want dollars, the dollar appreciates, U.S. goods become expensive and net exports fall. When the foreign real interest rate \(\bar{R}^w\) rises, the opposite happens:
\[\frac{NX_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \bar{a}_{nx} - \bar{b}_{nx}\,(R_t - \bar{R}^w). \qquad (20.6)\]
Adding and subtracting the marginal product of capital \(\bar{r}\) shows that net exports react to \(R_t - \bar{r}\) just like investment does. The IS curve keeps its old form, with two new pieces:
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}), \qquad \bar{b} \equiv \bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx}, \qquad
\bar{a} \equiv \bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{nx} - 1 + \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}). \qquad (20.8)\]
So a foreign interest rate above \(\bar{r}\) works as a positive aggregate demand shock \(\bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r})\). Combined with the policy rule of Chapter 13, the IS curve gives the AD curve \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\), and the Phillips curve gives the AS curve \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\).
One baseline for every diagram. The textbook draws its diagrams without numbers. Both model diagrams of this notebook start from one illustrative set of parameters:

marginal product of capital \(\bar{r} = 5\) percent, as in Chapter 11’s example, and no demand shock at home, \(\bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{nx} = 1\);
interest sensitivities \(\bar{b}_i = 1\) and \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 1\), so the total \(\bar{b} = 2\) is the value of Chapters 11 and 13, split half and half between investment and trade;
inflation target \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent, policy response \(\bar{m} = 1/2\) and Phillips-curve slope \(\bar{\nu} = 1\), as in Chapter 13;
the foreign shock of Figure 5: the foreign real interest rate is 2 points above \(\bar{r}\), at 7 percent, in periods 1 to 9 and back at \(\bar{r}\) afterwards.


Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing b_nx=B_NX gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. Names in capital letters, such as R_BAR, are constants that we set once and never change.


R_BAR, B_I, B_NX = 5.0, 1.0, 1.0            # marginal product of capital (%), interest sensitivities
PI_BAR, M_BAR, NU_BAR = 2.0, 0.5, 1.0       # inflation target (%), policy response, Phillips-curve slope
RW_GAP, A_LAST, T_MAX = 2.0, 9, 20          # foreign rate minus r_bar in periods 1-9; periods simulated


def long_run_exchange_rate(P_w, P):
    """Equation 20.3: the long-run nominal exchange rate E = P_w / P (foreign currency per dollar)."""
    return P_w / P


def real_exchange_rate(E, P, P_w):
    """The real exchange rate E P / P_w: foreign goods needed to buy one U.S. good (equation 20.4)."""
    return E * P / P_w


def net_exports(R, R_w=R_BAR, a_nx=0.0, b_nx=B_NX):
    """Equation 20.6: net exports in percent of potential output, NX/Y = a_nx - b_nx (R - R_w)."""
    return a_nx - b_nx * (R - R_w)


def foreign_shock(R_w, b_nx=B_NX, r_bar=R_BAR):
    """The part of a_bar that comes from abroad in equation 20.8: b_nx (R_w - r_bar)."""
    return b_nx * (R_w - r_bar)


def is_curve(R, a=0.0, b_i=B_I, b_nx=B_NX, r_bar=R_BAR):
    """Equation 20.8, the open-economy IS curve: Y~ = a - (b_i + b_nx) (R - r_bar), in percent."""
    return a - (b_i + b_nx) * (R - r_bar)


def ad_output(pi, a=0.0, m=M_BAR, b=B_I + B_NX):
    """The AD curve of Chapter 13 with the open-economy b: Y~ = a - b m (pi - pi_bar)."""
    return a - b * m * (pi - PI_BAR)


def as_inflation(Y, pi_e, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The AS curve of Chapter 13: pi = pi_e + nu Y~, with expected inflation pi_e = last period's inflation."""
    return pi_e + nu * Y


def solve_asad(pi_e, a=0.0, m=M_BAR, b=B_I + B_NX, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The point where the AD and AS curves cross: short-run output and inflation in one period."""
    Y = (a - b * m * (pi_e - PI_BAR)) / (1 + b * m * nu)
    return Y, as_inflation(Y, pi_e, nu)

Let us try the functions on a few textbook cases.

Python note. An f-string such as f"E = {E:.2f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.2f means “show two decimals” and :+.1f also shows the sign. Y, pi = solve_asad(...) unpacks the two results of the function into two variables.


E = long_run_exchange_rate(P_w=92.0, P=100.0)       # a chip costs 92 euros in Germany and 100 dollars in the U.S.
print(f"Law of one price: E = {E:.2f} euros per dollar")
print(f"Real exchange rate at that E: {real_exchange_rate(E, 100.0, 92.0):.2f}; at E = 1.00: "
      f"{real_exchange_rate(1.0, 100.0, 92.0):.2f}")
print(f"Net exports when R rises from 5% to 6%: {net_exports(6.0):+.1f}% of potential output")
print(f"IS curve at R = 6%: Y~ = {is_curve(6.0):+.1f}% (without the trade channel: {is_curve(6.0, b_nx=0.0):+.1f}%)")
a = foreign_shock(R_BAR + RW_GAP)
Y, pi = solve_asad(PI_BAR, a)
print(f"Foreign rate 2 points above r_bar: a = {a:.1f}; first period Y~ = {Y:+.2f}%, inflation = {pi:.2f}%")

At 0.92 euros per dollar the chip costs the same in both countries, so the real exchange rate is 1. At 1 euro per dollar U.S. chips are about 9 percent too expensive. With the trade channel, a 1-point rise in the interest rate lowers output by 2 percent instead of 1. And a foreign interest rate 2 points above \(\bar{r}\) is a demand shock of \(\bar{a} = 2\): the same shock as Chapter 13’s aggregate demand shock, so the same dynamics follow.

One loop for the dynamics
Figure 5 follows the economy period by period. Each period, firms expect last period’s inflation, and the economy jumps to the point where that period’s AD and AS curves cross. simulate repeats this step; shock_list builds the list of demand shocks, one value per period.

Python note. values.append(x) adds x at the end of the list values, and for t in range(1, 21) repeats the indented lines for t = 1, 2, …, 20. dict(period=0, Y=0.0) is a dictionary, a set of named values, and rows[-1]["pi"] is the value named "pi" in the last element of the list. pd.DataFrame(rows) turns a list of dictionaries into a table, one row per dictionary.


def shock_list(size, last=A_LAST):
    """A demand shock of the given size in periods 1, ..., last and zero afterwards, for T_MAX periods."""
    values = []
    for t in range(1, T_MAX + 1):
        if t <= last:
            values.append(size)
        else:
            values.append(0.0)
    return values


def simulate(a_list, m=M_BAR, b=B_I + B_NX, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Solve the AS/AD model period by period; period 0 is the steady state (Y~ = 0, pi = pi_bar)."""
    rows = [dict(period=0, a=0.0, pi_e=PI_BAR, Y=0.0, pi=PI_BAR)]
    for t in range(1, len(a_list) + 1):
        pi_e = rows[-1]["pi"]                   # adaptive expectations: last period's inflation
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, a_list[t - 1], m, b, nu)
        rows.append(dict(period=t, a=a_list[t - 1], pi_e=pi_e, Y=Y, pi=pi))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


simulate(shock_list(2.0)).loc[[0, 1, 2, 8, 9, 10, 11]].round(3)

Inflation rises from 2 to 3 percent in period 1 and climbs toward 4 percent while the shock lasts. When the shock ends in period 10, output falls below potential and inflation starts back down to 2 percent.


Drawing tools
Both model diagrams use the same few drawing steps, so we write them once:

add_curve draws a curve and writes its name at its last point inside the axes, as the textbook does;
add_point marks a point with a dot, a letter and dashed guides to the axes;
add_arrow draws an arrow between two points.


Python note. (x >= 0) & (y <= 8) is true where both conditions hold, x[inside] keeps the values where inside is true, and [-1] takes the last of them. add_annotation with axref="x" and ayref="y" draws an arrow from (ax, ay) to (x, y), both in axis units. Labels such as "AS<sub>8</sub>" use HTML to write AS₈.


def add_curve(fig, x, y, label, color, x_range, y_range, dash="solid"):
    """Draw one curve and write its label at its last point inside the axes (no label if label is "")."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)))
    inside = (x >= x_range[0]) & (x <= x_range[1]) & (y >= y_range[0]) & (y <= y_range[1])
    if inside.any() and label != "":
        fig.add_annotation(x=x[inside][-1], y=y[inside][-1], text=label, showarrow=False,
                           xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", font=dict(color=color, size=14))


def add_point(fig, x, y, label, x0, y0, guides=True):
    """Mark the point (x, y) with a dot and a label; with guides, dashed lines to the axes at x0 and y0."""
    if guides:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x0, x, x], y=[y, y, y0], mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                                 line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x], y=[y], mode="markers+text", text=[label], textposition="top right",
                             name=label, showlegend=False, textfont=dict(size=16), marker=dict(color="black", size=10)))


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, color="black"):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) in axis units; nothing if the two points almost coincide."""
    if abs(x1 - x0) + abs(y1 - y0) > 0.15:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x1, y=y1, ax=x0, ay=y0, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y", text="",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor=color)

title: Chapter 20: Exchange Rates and International Finance
section: Figure 1: The U.S. exchange rate versus the yen and the euro
text:
Figure 1: The U.S. exchange rate versus the yen and the euro
Goal. See how the price of a dollar has moved since the end of fixed exchange rates in 1971.
The exchange rate here is the price of a dollar in foreign currency: how many yen, or how many euros, one dollar buys. A fall is a depreciation of the dollar, a rise an appreciation. The two series have very different units (hundreds of yen, about one euro), so the textbook draws them on two vertical scales.

Python note. parse_dates=["date"] tells read_csv that the column date holds dates, so Plotly draws a proper time axis. .tail() shows the last five rows. The euro only exists since 1999, so the column eur_per_usd is empty (NaN, “not a number”) before that.


fx = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig20-1.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
fx.tail()

Each row is a month: yen_per_usd is the average number of yen per dollar, and eur_per_usd the number of euros per dollar (the Federal Reserve publishes dollars per euro; the data file turns it around so that both lines are the price of a dollar).

Python note. px.line draws the yen line. add_scatter(..., yaxis="y2") adds the euro line on a second vertical axis, which yaxis2=dict(overlaying="y", side="right") places on the right. hovermode="x unified" shows both values of the month you point at in one box.


fig = px.line(fx, x="date", y="yen_per_usd", labels={"date": "Year", "yen_per_usd": "Yen per dollar"},
              title="Yen per dollar: 358 in 1971, 84 in 1995, between 76 and 162 since then")
fig.update_traces(line_color=BLUE, name="Yen per dollar")
fig.add_scatter(x=fx.date, y=fx.eur_per_usd, name="Euros per dollar", yaxis="y2", line=dict(color=TEAL))
fig.update_layout(showlegend=False, hovermode="x unified",
                  xaxis=dict(range=["1970-01-01", "2028-01-01"]),
                  yaxis=dict(title="Yen per dollar (left scale)", range=[50, 400], color=BLUE),
                  yaxis2=dict(title="Euros per dollar (right scale)", range=[0.6, 1.3], color=TEAL,
                              overlaying="y", side="right", showgrid=False))
fig.add_annotation(x="1981-06-01", y=335, text="Yen per dollar<br>(left scale)", showarrow=False,
                   font=dict(color=BLUE, size=14))
fig.add_annotation(x="2010-01-01", y=1.2, yref="y2", text="Euros per dollar<br>(right scale)", showarrow=False,
                   font=dict(color=TEAL, size=14))
fig.show()

What to notice.

From 1971 to 1995 the dollar lost three quarters of its value against the yen: from 358 yen in January 1971 to 84 in April 1995.
Against the euro the dollar first appreciated, to 1.17 euros in October 2000, then depreciated to 0.63 in July 2008, and has been between about 0.8 and 1.0 euros in most years since 2015.
The newest data go beyond the textbook: in 2024–2026 the dollar bought 143 to 162 yen. The 162 yen of July 2026 are the most since 1986.


Key numbers: the dates in the text

Python note. fx.set_index("date") uses the dates as row labels, and .loc[...] picks rows by label. pd.to_datetime([...]) turns a list of texts into dates, so that they match the row labels.


months = pd.to_datetime(["1971-01-01", "1995-04-01", "1995-07-01", "2023-05-01",
                         "1999-03-01", "2002-02-01", "2008-07-01", "2026-09-01"])
fx.set_index("date").loc[months].round(3)

The textbook’s numbers are all here: 357 (358) yen in 1971, 87 in mid-1995, 137 in early 2023; 0.92 euros in 1999, 1.15 at the start of 2002 and the low of 0.64 in 2008.
Your turn. Find the month in which the dollar bought the fewest yen, and the month in which it bought the most euros.


Hint

fx.yen_per_usd.idxmin() gives the row number of the smallest value, and fx.loc[row] shows that row. Use idxmax() for the euro.

section: Figure 2: Inflation in the United States and Japan
text:
Figure 2: Inflation in the United States and Japan
Goal. Check the law of one price’s prediction: if the dollar depreciated against the yen for decades, U.S. inflation must have been higher than Japan’s.
Write equation (20.3) in growth rates. With \(E\) = yen per dollar, \(P^w\) the Japanese and \(P\) the U.S. price level,
\[\frac{\Delta \bar{E}}{\bar{E}} \approx \pi^{w} - \pi,\]
so the dollar loses value against the yen by roughly the gap between U.S. and Japanese inflation.

inflation = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig20-2.csv")
inflation.tail()

The columns are annual consumer-price inflation, in percent. The U.S. value for 2025 is not published yet (NaN). After melt we drop that empty row with .dropna(), so that it does not break the line.

Python note. rename(columns={...}) gives the columns readable names, which then appear in the legend. melt(id_vars="year") turns the two country columns into rows: one row per year and country, with the old column name in country and the value in inflation. That long shape is what px.line(..., color="country") needs.


long = inflation.rename(columns={"inflation_us": "United States", "inflation_jpn": "Japan"})
long = long.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="country", value_name="inflation").dropna()
fig = px.line(long, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", hover_name="country",
              color_discrete_map={"United States": BLUE, "Japan": TEAL},
              labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation (percent per year)", "country": ""},
              title="Inflation was higher in the United States than in Japan in most years")
fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
fig.update_layout(yaxis_range=[-3, 25], legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
fig.show()

What to notice.

Japan’s inflation jumped to 23 percent in 1974, after the first oil shock; U.S. inflation peaked at 13.5 percent in 1980.
From the late 1990s Japan had deflation in many years (falling prices), while U.S. inflation stayed positive except in 2009.
Click a country in the legend to hide it, and hover over the lines to read the values.


Key numbers: average inflation

for first, last in [(1971, 1995), (1996, 2024), (1971, 2024)]:
    span = inflation[(inflation.year >= first) & (inflation.year <= last)]
    us, jp = span.inflation_us.mean(), span.inflation_jpn.mean()
    print(f"{first}–{last}: United States {us:.2f}%, Japan {jp:.2f}%, gap {us - jp:.2f} points a year")

Between 1971 and 1995 U.S. inflation was higher by only about 1 point a year, as the textbook says. Figure 3 shows why that small gap cannot explain the dollar’s fall from 358 to 84 yen.


Table 20.1: the Big Mac index
The Economist compares the price of a Big Mac around the world. If the law of one price held for burgers, a Big Mac would cost the same number of dollars everywhere. The data file big_mac.csv holds every release of the index since 2000, made by data/ch20/build_data.py from The Economist’s open data.

big_mac = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "big_mac.csv")
big_mac.head()

Each row is one economy in one release: the local price, the market exchange rate (local currency per dollar) and the dollar price, local price / exchange rate. gdp_pc_2023 is GDP per person from the Penn World Table, which we use in Figure 3.

Python note. set_index("country") uses the country names as row labels, and .loc[BOOK_ROWS] picks the rows in the order of the list. A new column is created simply by assigning to it: table["vs_US_percent"] = ....


BOOK_ROWS = ["United States", "Norway", "Euro area", "Mexico", "China", "Japan", "South Africa", "India"]


def big_mac_table(release="2022-07-01"):
    """Table 20.1: Big Mac prices in local currency and in dollars, for one release of the index."""
    table = big_mac[big_mac.release == release].set_index("country").loc[BOOK_ROWS]
    us_price = table.loc["United States", "dollar_price"]
    table["vs_US_percent"] = 100 * (table.dollar_price / us_price - 1)      # dearer (+) or cheaper (-) than in the U.S.
    return table[["local_price", "currency", "ex_rate", "dollar_price", "vs_US_percent"]].round(2)


table = big_mac_table("2022-07-01")
table["textbook"] = pd.Series({"United States": 5.15, "Norway": 6.26, "Euro area": 4.74, "Mexico": 3.43,
                               "China": 3.56, "Japan": 2.83, "South Africa": 2.34, "India": 2.39})
table

The textbook’s table is the release of July 2022, and every dollar price matches. The one exception, the euro area, is only rounding: the textbook divides 4.65 euros by a rounded 0.98 euros per dollar. Always look at what a data series measures: India’s row is not a beef Big Mac at all but the chicken Maharaja Mac, since McDonald’s in India sells no beef.
What to notice.

The law of one price clearly fails for Big Macs: from 2.34 dollars in South Africa to 6.26 dollars in Norway.
By the burger standard, Norway’s krone was overvalued (21.6 percent dearer than in the U.S.) and China’s yuan undervalued (30.9 percent cheaper).

section: Figure 3: The real exchange rate for Japan
text:
Figure 3: The real exchange rate for Japan
Goal. See that the real exchange rate can move for decades, and learn one reason why: the Balassa-Samuelson effect.
The real exchange rate from Japan’s point of view is the price of Japanese goods in units of U.S. goods. With \(E\) in yen per dollar, Japanese goods cost \(P^{Japan}/E\) dollars, so
\[RER^{Japan} = \frac{P^{Japan}/E}{P^{US}}.\]
The textbook uses the Penn World Table, which compares the price of GDP in the two countries, as an index with 1971 = 100.

rer = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig20-3.csv")
rer.tail()

We can also build the real exchange rate ourselves, from the data of Figures 1 and 2. Inflation tells us how fast the price level grows each year, so multiplying the growth factors \(1 + \pi_t/100\) year after year gives the price level.

Python note. fx.date.dt.year takes the year out of each date, and groupby("year").yen_per_usd.mean() averages the 12 months of each year. .cumprod() is the cumulative product: it multiplies the growth factors year after year, \(P_t = P_{t-1}(1+\pi_t/100)\). Dividing two pandas series lines up their rows by year automatically.


fx["year"] = fx.date.dt.year
yen = fx.groupby("year").yen_per_usd.mean()              # annual average, yen per dollar

prices = inflation[inflation.year >= 1971].set_index("year")
growth_us = 1 + prices.inflation_us / 100
growth_jp = 1 + prices.inflation_jpn / 100
P_us = growth_us.cumprod() / growth_us.loc[1971]          # consumer price level, 1971 = 1
P_jp = growth_jp.cumprod() / growth_jp.loc[1971]

estimate = (P_jp / yen) / P_us                            # dollar price of Japanese goods relative to U.S. goods
estimate = (100 * estimate / estimate.loc[1971]).dropna()  # index, 1971 = 100
estimate.loc[[1971, 1995, 2023, 2024]].round(1)


Python note. pd.DataFrame({...}) builds a table from a dictionary of series, one column each, lined up by year. line_dash="measure" draws the two measures with different dash styles.


compare = pd.DataFrame({"Penn World Table (GDP prices)": rer.set_index("year").rer_jpn,
                        "Our estimate (consumer prices)": estimate})
compare.index.name = "year"
compare = compare.reset_index().melt(id_vars="year", var_name="measure", value_name="rer").dropna()
fig = px.line(compare, x="year", y="rer", color="measure", line_dash="measure", hover_name="measure",
              color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL], range_y=[50, 320],
              labels={"year": "Year", "rer": "Real exchange rate of Japan (1971 = 100)", "measure": ""},
              title="Japan's real exchange rate rose 2.5-fold from 1971 to 1995, then fell back")
fig.add_hline(y=100, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
fig.show()

What to notice.

Japanese goods became much more expensive relative to U.S. goods until 1995: the Penn World Table index peaks at

Since then they have become cheaper again, and in 2022–2023 the index fell below its 1971 level.

Our consumer-price estimate rises more (to 286 in 1995), because it compares consumer prices rather than the prices of everything an economy produces, but it tells the same story year by year.


Key numbers: the law of one price, 1971–1995
If the law of one price had held, the yen-dollar rate would have changed each year only by the inflation gap. We apply the growth factors of 1972–1995 to the 1971 rate.

Python note. .prod() multiplies all the values of a series, here the 24 yearly factors.


years = inflation[(inflation.year >= 1972) & (inflation.year <= 1995)]
ratio = ((1 + years.inflation_jpn / 100) / (1 + years.inflation_us / 100)).prod()
print(f"Yen per dollar, 1971 average:                     {yen[1971]:.0f}")
print(f"1995 rate predicted by the law of one price:      {yen[1971] * ratio:.0f}")
print(f"Actual 1995 average:                              {yen[1995]:.0f}")

The inflation gap explains a fall to about 269 yen per dollar. The dollar actually fell to 94 yen, so the real exchange rate of the yen rose a lot. That is the “apparent contradiction” of the textbook’s case study.


The Balassa-Samuelson effect in the Big Mac data
The explanation is that only traded goods obey the law of one price. Haircuts and restaurant meals cannot be shipped, and their prices follow local wages. As an economy grows, wages rise, nontraded goods become dearer, and the real exchange rate appreciates. So richer countries should have dearer Big Macs (the burger includes the work of the staff and the rent of the restaurant). We check this with the latest Big Mac release and GDP per person.

latest = big_mac[big_mac.release == big_mac.release.max()].dropna(subset=["gdp_pc_2023"])
latest.sort_values("gdp_pc_2023").head(3)

Look at the first row. GDP per person in Venezuela appears to be about 160 dollars a year, which is not plausible: during Venezuela’s hyperinflation the price data behind this number broke down (we met the same problem in Chapter 5). We drop Venezuela, and label only the economies of Table 20.1.

Python note. log_x=True puts GDP per person on a ratio scale, and trendline="ols" adds the best-fitting straight line. trendline_options=dict(log_x=True) fits that line to the logarithm of GDP, so that it is straight on the ratio scale. .where(condition, "") keeps a value where the condition holds and puts "" elsewhere.


latest = latest[latest.iso3 != "VEN"].copy()
latest["label"] = latest.country.where(latest.country.isin(BOOK_ROWS), "")
fig = px.scatter(latest, x="gdp_pc_2023", y="dollar_price", text="label", hover_name="country", log_x=True,
                 trendline="ols", trendline_options=dict(log_x=True), range_x=[4000, 150000], range_y=[0, 10],
                 labels={"gdp_pc_2023": "GDP per person, 2023 (2021 dollars, ratio scale)",
                         "dollar_price": "Price of a Big Mac in dollars (July 2026)"},
                 title="Big Macs cost more in richer countries: the Balassa-Samuelson effect")
fig.update_traces(textposition="top center", marker=dict(size=9, color=TEAL))
fig.show()

What to notice.

The fitted line slopes up: a Big Mac costs about 2 dollars more for every tenfold rise in GDP per person. Indonesia, India and the Philippines are cheap; Switzerland, Uruguay and Norway are the dearest.
The cloud is wide. Japan and Taiwan are rich but have cheap Big Macs. For Japan this is the weak yen of 2026, the fall of the real exchange rate in the figure above.

Your turn. Redo the scatter for the release of July 2012. Is the slope steeper or flatter than in 2026?


Hint

Replace big_mac.release.max() with "2012-07-01" in the first cell, then rerun the drop of Venezuela and the chart. Hover over the fitted line to read its equation.

title: Chapter 20: Exchange Rates and International Finance
section: Figure 4: Increasing interest rates and the IS curve
text:
Figure 4: Increasing interest rates and the IS curve
Goal. See why the IS curve is flatter in an open economy: a higher interest rate lowers net exports as well as investment.
The central bank raises the real interest rate from \(\bar{r}\) to \(R'\). The economy moves along the IS curve from \(A\) to \(B\). Two forces lower output:
\[\uparrow R \;\Rightarrow\; \downarrow \frac{I}{\bar{Y}} \quad\text{and}\quad
\uparrow R \Rightarrow \uparrow E \Rightarrow \uparrow \frac{EP}{P^w} \Rightarrow \downarrow \frac{NX}{\bar{Y}}.\]
From equation (20.8), \(\tilde{Y}' = -(\bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx})(R' - \bar{r})\). The dashed gray line is the IS curve without the trade channel (\(\bar{b}_{nx} = 0\)), the closed economy of Chapter 11.

R_LINE = np.linspace(9, 2, 141)              # real interest rates, high to low, at which we draw the IS curves
X_IS, R_AXIS = [-11, 5], [2, 9]              # fixed axes, so that you can see the curve turn


def tightening(R_new=6.0, b_nx=B_NX, b_i=B_I):
    """Figure 20.4: the central bank raises R from r_bar to R_new; the economy moves along the IS curve."""
    Y_new = is_curve(R_new, b_i=b_i, b_nx=b_nx)
    fig = go.Figure()
    if b_nx > 0:
        add_curve(fig, is_curve(R_LINE, b_i=b_i, b_nx=0.0), R_LINE, "IS without trade", GRAY, X_IS, R_AXIS, "dash")
    add_curve(fig, is_curve(R_LINE, b_i=b_i, b_nx=b_nx), R_LINE, "IS", BLUE, X_IS, R_AXIS)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", X_IS[0], R_AXIS[0])
    add_point(fig, Y_new, R_new, "B", X_IS[0], R_AXIS[0])
    add_arrow(fig, X_IS[0] + 0.6, R_BAR, X_IS[0] + 0.6, R_new)              # the interest rate rises ...
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, R_AXIS[0] + 0.3, Y_new, R_AXIS[0] + 0.3)            # ... and output falls
    invest = -b_i * (R_new - R_BAR) + 0.0                                    # + 0.0 avoids printing -0.0
    trade = -b_nx * (R_new - R_BAR) + 0.0
    fig.update_layout(title=f"R′ = {R_new:.1f}%  →  Ỹ′ = {Y_new + 0.0:.1f}%   "
                            f"(investment {invest:.1f}, net exports {trade:.1f})",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)", range=X_IS, tickvals=list(range(-10, 5, 2)),
                                 zeroline=False),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Real interest rate, R (percent)", range=R_AXIS, tickvals=list(range(3, 9)),
                                 zeroline=False))
    return fig


Python note. interact turns each argument of a function into a slider and calls the function again every time you move one. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.


interact(tightening,
         R_new=FloatSlider(value=6.0, min=4.0, max=7.5, step=0.5, description="new real interest rate R′ (%)", style=WIDE),
         b_nx=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.0, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="net-export sensitivity b̄ₙₓ", style=WIDE),
         b_i=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="investment sensitivity b̄ᵢ", style=WIDE));



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Figure 4 with a precomputed slider for the net-export sensitivity
slider_figure(tightening, "b_nx", [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0], start=1.0, label="net-export sensitivity b̄ₙₓ")


What to notice.

With the baseline, raising \(R\) from 5 to 6 percent lowers output by 2 percent: 1 point through investment and 1 point through net exports. Without trade, output would fall by only 1 percent.
Raise \(\bar{b}_{nx}\): the IS curve turns flatter and point \(B\) moves left. The more net exports react to the exchange rate, the more powerful monetary policy is.
Nothing else changes: the curve still passes through \(A\), because at \(R = \bar{r}\) there is no gap to react to.

Hint

Output falls by \((\bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx})\) percent per point. Try is_curve(6.0, b_nx=2.0).

title: Chapter 20: Exchange Rates and International Finance
section: Figure 5: An increase in foreign interest rates
text:
Figure 5: An increase in foreign interest rates
Goal. Follow the international transmission of monetary policy: the European Central Bank raises its interest rate, and the U.S. economy booms, then slumps.
When the foreign real interest rate rises to \(\bar{R}^w = 7\) percent, 2 points above \(\bar{r}\), investors move from dollars to euros, the dollar depreciates, U.S. goods become cheap and U.S. net exports rise. In equation (20.8) this is a positive demand shock, \(\bar{a} = \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}) = 2\), so the AD curve shifts out to AD₁. Then the familiar dynamics of Chapter 13 take over:

period 1: the economy jumps from \(A\) to \(B\), with output and inflation above normal;
periods 2–9: inflation rises, the Fed raises U.S. interest rates, and the economy climbs AD₁ toward \(C\) (period 8 in the textbook), with output back at potential but inflation above target;
period 10: the foreign rate falls back to \(\bar{r}\), the shock ends, AD shifts back, and the economy drops to a recession at \(D\); it then slides down AD back to \(A\).

The function draws period t: the original AS curve, the AS curve of period t, both AD curves (the one that holds in period t in full color), the path so far with the textbook’s letters, and the path still to come in gray.

Y_LINE = np.linspace(-6, 6, 121)                # output levels at which we draw the AS curves
PI_LINE = np.linspace(12, -4, 161)              # inflation rates, high to low, at which we draw the AD curves
X_AD, PI_AXIS = [-3.5, 3.5], [-0.5, 7.5]        # fixed axes
LETTERS = {0: "A", 1: "B", 8: "C", 10: "D"}     # the textbook's letters for periods 0, 1, 8 and 10
FADED = "rgba(22,82,140,0.35)"                  # light blue for the AD curve that does not hold in period t


def add_asad_curves(fig, a, pi_e, t, m, b):
    """The AS curves (original and period t) and the AD curves (original and shifted) of Figure 5."""
    add_curve(fig, Y_LINE, as_inflation(Y_LINE, PI_BAR), "AS", TEAL, X_AD, PI_AXIS)
    if abs(pi_e - PI_BAR) > 0.05:                                   # skip the AS of period t if it is the old one
        label = f"AS<sub>{t}</sub>" if abs(pi_e - PI_BAR) > 0.6 else ""
        add_curve(fig, Y_LINE, as_inflation(Y_LINE, pi_e), label, TEAL, X_AD, PI_AXIS)
    shock_on = 1 <= t <= A_LAST
    ad_label = f"AD = AD<sub>{t}</sub>" if t > A_LAST else "AD"
    add_curve(fig, ad_output(PI_LINE, 0.0, m, b), PI_LINE, ad_label, FADED if shock_on else BLUE, X_AD, PI_AXIS)
    if a != 0:
        label = "AD<sub>1</sub>" if abs(a / (b * m)) > 0.6 else ""  # no label when it would sit on AD's label
        add_curve(fig, ad_output(PI_LINE, a, m, b), PI_LINE, label, BLUE if shock_on else FADED, X_AD, PI_AXIS)


def add_path(fig, path, t):
    """The economy's path up to period t (dots, arrows, letters) and the rest of the path in gray."""
    future = path[path.period >= t]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=future.Y, y=future.pi, mode="lines+markers", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=1, dash="dot"), marker=dict(color=GRAY, size=5)))
    for s in range(1, t + 1):
        add_arrow(fig, path.Y[s - 1], path.pi[s - 1], path.Y[s], path.pi[s])
    for s in range(t + 1):
        if s in LETTERS:
            add_point(fig, path.Y[s], path.pi[s], LETTERS[s], X_AD[0], PI_AXIS[0], guides=False)


def foreign_rate_shock(gap=RW_GAP, t=10, b_nx=B_NX, m=M_BAR):
    """Figure 20.5: period t after the foreign real interest rate rises gap points above r_bar in periods 1-9."""
    a = foreign_shock(R_BAR + gap, b_nx)                 # equation 20.8: the demand shock from abroad
    b = B_I + b_nx
    path = simulate(shock_list(a), m, b)
    now = path.loc[t]
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_asad_curves(fig, a, now.pi_e, t, m, b)
    add_path(fig, path, t)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Period {t}: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {round(now.Y, 2) + 0.0:+.2f}%   "
                            f"(Rʷ − r̄ = {gap:.1f}, so ā = {a:.1f} in periods 1–{A_LAST})",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Output, Ỹ (percent)", range=X_AD, tickvals=list(range(-3, 4)), zeroline=False),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Inflation, π (percent)", range=PI_AXIS, tickvals=list(range(0, 8)), zeroline=False))
    return fig


Python note. IntSlider is a slider for whole numbers, here the period t. path.loc[t] is the row of period t, and now.pi is its value in the column pi.


interact(foreign_rate_shock,
         gap=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=3.0, step=0.5, description="foreign rate gap Rʷ − r̄", style=WIDE),
         t=IntSlider(value=10, min=1, max=20, step=1, description="period t", style=WIDE),
         b_nx=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.5, description="net-export sensitivity b̄ₙₓ", style=WIDE),
         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE));



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Figure 5 with a precomputed slider for the period
slider_figure(foreign_rate_shock, "t", [1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 10, 12, 20], start=10, label="period t")


What to notice.

At \(B\) (period 1) output is 1 percent above potential and inflation 3 percent: half of the shock goes into output, half into inflation, because \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1\) as in Chapter 13.
At \(C\) output is back at potential, but inflation is close to \(\bar{\pi} + \bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m}) = 4\) percent. The AS curves of periods 8, 9 and 10 are almost the same line, which is why the textbook draws \(C\) and \(D\) on one curve, AS₈.
When the shock ends, the economy pays for the boom with a recession at \(D\): output 1 percent below potential.
The U.S. did nothing, yet its economy boomed and slumped: a change in interest rates abroad is a demand shock at home.

Your turn. Suppose the ECB cuts its interest rate instead. You cannot set a negative gap with the slider, so use the code: simulate a gap of \(-2\) and describe the path of output and inflation in periods 1, 8 and 10.


Hint

simulate(shock_list(foreign_shock(R_BAR - 2.0))) gives the whole path. The pattern is the mirror image of the one above.

text:
Figure 6: The U.K.-U.S. exchange rate
Goal. Read two centuries of exchange-rate history in one line: the gold standard, Bretton Woods and floating rates.
Under the gold standard each country fixed the price of an ounce of gold in its currency. From 1834 the United States paid about 20.67 dollars an ounce and the United Kingdom 4.25 pounds, so a dollar was worth \(4.25/20.67 \approx 0.206\) pounds. Under Bretton Woods (1944 to the early 1970s) other currencies were pegged to the dollar, and the dollar to gold at 35 dollars an ounce. Since 1973 the major currencies float.

uk = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig20-6.csv")
uk.head()


Python note. px.area draws a line and fills the area below it. add_hline draws a horizontal reference line across the whole figure; annotation_text writes a short text next to it.


fig = px.area(uk, x="year", y="gbp_per_usd", labels={"year": "Year", "gbp_per_usd": "Pounds per dollar"},
              range_x=[1785, 2030], range_y=[0.1, 0.9],
              title="Pounds per dollar: fixed under gold, steps under Bretton Woods, floating since 1973")
fig.update_traces(line_color=BLUE, fillcolor="rgba(138,150,163,0.25)", hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.3f} pounds")
fig.add_hline(y=4.25 / 20.67, line_dash="dot", line_color=TEAL, annotation_text="gold parity 0.206",
              annotation_position="bottom right", annotation_font_color=TEAL)
fig.add_annotation(x=1855, y=0.25, text="Gold standard", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=14))
fig.add_annotation(x=1937, y=0.43, text="Bretton<br>Woods", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=14))
fig.add_annotation(x=1997, y=0.42, text="Floating<br>exchange rates", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=14))
fig.show()

What to notice.

For most of the 19th century the line is flat at the gold parity. The exception is the Civil War: the U.S. left gold, and in 1864 the dollar fell to 0.100 pounds, half its value.
Bretton Woods shows up as long flat steps: 0.357 pounds (2.80 dollars per pound) in the 1950s and 1960s, 0.417 (2.40 dollars) after the pound’s devaluation in 1967.
Since 1973 the line moves a lot every year. And over the two centuries the dollar appreciated, from 0.22 pounds in 1791 to 0.76 in 2025, as the U.S. economy overtook the British one.


Key numbers: how stable is each regime?
We measure stability by the typical yearly change of the exchange rate: the standard deviation of its percent changes.

Python note. .pct_change() computes the percent change from one row to the next (here, from one year to the next), and .std() the standard deviation, the typical size of the changes. A dictionary maps each name to a pair of years, and first, last = REGIMES[name] unpacks the pair.


print(f"Gold parity: 4.25 / 20.67 = {4.25 / 20.67:.4f} pounds per dollar")
REGIMES = {"Gold standard, 1880–1913": (1880, 1913), "Bretton Woods, 1951–1966": (1951, 1966),
           "Floating rates, 1974–2025": (1974, 2025)}
rate = uk.set_index("year").gbp_per_usd
changes = 100 * rate.pct_change()
for name in REGIMES:
    first, last = REGIMES[name]
    print(f"{name}: average {rate.loc[first:last].mean():.3f} pounds per dollar, "
          f"typical yearly change {changes.loc[first:last].std():.2f}%")

Under the gold standard and Bretton Woods the exchange rate typically moved by less than half a percent a year; with floating rates, by more than 8 percent.
Your turn. The textbook’s case study says the dollar fell sharply during the Civil War. By how many percent did it fall from 1860 to 1864, and in which year was it back at the gold parity?


Hint

rate.loc[1860:1880] shows the years around the war. The percent change is 100 * (rate[1864] / rate[1860] - 1).

title: Chapter 20: Exchange Rates and International Finance
section: Figure 7: The policy trilemma in open economies
text:
Figure 7: The policy trilemma in open economies
Goal. See why an open economy can have at most two of three good things: a stable exchange rate, its own monetary policy, and free flows of international finance.
The textbook draws the policy trilemma as a triangle: the three goals are its corners, and each side is a regime that achieves the two goals at its ends and gives up the one opposite. Here the triangle is live. A small model from the chapter computes what happens when the foreign central bank (say, the Fed) raises its interest rate by \(\Delta i^w\), while your economy needs its own interest rate to change by \(\Delta i^{need}\):

with free financial flows, the exchange rate moves with the interest gap (Section 20.3: \(\uparrow i \Rightarrow \uparrow E\)), \(\%\Delta E = \eta\,(\Delta i - \Delta i^w)\), with an illustrative \(\eta = 5\) percent per point;
floating exchange rate: the central bank sets \(\Delta i = \Delta i^{need}\), and the exchange rate moves;
currency board (or monetary union): to keep \(E\) fixed, the interest rate must follow abroad, \(\Delta i = \Delta i^w\);
capital controls: the central bank sets \(\Delta i = \Delta i^{need}\) and keeps \(E\) fixed, because it rations the trade in its currency, so money cannot flow freely.


ETA = 5.0                                       # percent change of E per point of interest gap (illustrative)
LOST = {"floating exchange rate": "stable exchange rate", "currency board": "monetary autonomy",
        "capital controls": "free financial flows"}     # the goal each regime gives up: the opposite corner


def trilemma_outcome(regime, di_world, di_need):
    """Figure 20.7 as a model: the change in the domestic interest rate and the percent change in E."""
    if regime == "currency board":
        di = di_world                           # the peg forces the domestic rate to follow the foreign rate
    else:
        di = di_need                            # floating or capital controls: the central bank chooses
    if regime == "floating exchange rate":
        dE = ETA * (di - di_world)              # free capital flows move the exchange rate
    else:
        dE = 0.0                                # fixed by the peg, or by rationing the currency
    return di, dE + 0.0, LOST[regime]


print(trilemma_outcome("floating exchange rate", 1.0, 0.0))
print(trilemma_outcome("currency board", 1.0, 0.0))


CORNERS = {"stable exchange rate": (1.0, 1.732), "monetary autonomy": (0.0, 0.0), "free financial flows": (2.0, 0.0)}
CORNER_TEXT = {"stable exchange rate": (1.0, 1.95, "Stable exchange rate"),
               "monetary autonomy": (0.0, -0.22, "Monetary policy<br>autonomy"),
               "free financial flows": (2.0, -0.22, "Free financial<br>flows")}
SIDES = {"floating exchange rate": ("monetary autonomy", "free financial flows", 1.0, -0.1, 0),
         "currency board": ("stable exchange rate", "free financial flows", 1.62, 0.96, 60),
         "capital controls": ("monetary autonomy", "stable exchange rate", 0.38, 0.96, -60)}
SIDE_TEXT = {"floating exchange rate": "Floating exchange rate", "currency board": "Monetary union or currency board",
             "capital controls": "Capital controls"}

The four dictionaries above hold the geometry: the corners of the triangle, where each label goes, and which two corners each side joins (with its label position and angle). draw_triangle uses them.

def draw_triangle(fig, regime):
    """The trilemma triangle: the chosen side thick and green, the goal it gives up marked with a gray cross."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, 2, 1, 0], y=[0, 0, 1.732, 0], fill="toself", fillcolor="#e6f5f1", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2), showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip"))
    for side in SIDES:
        start, end, x, y, angle = SIDES[side]
        chosen = side == regime
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[CORNERS[start][0], CORNERS[end][0]], y=[CORNERS[start][1], CORNERS[end][1]],
                                 mode="lines", line=dict(color=GREEN if chosen else GRAY, width=9 if chosen else 2),
                                 name=SIDE_TEXT[side], showlegend=False))
        fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=SIDE_TEXT[side], textangle=angle, showarrow=False,
                           font=dict(size=13, color=TEAL if chosen else GRAY))
    for goal in CORNERS:
        kept = goal != LOST[regime]
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[CORNERS[goal][0]], y=[CORNERS[goal][1]], mode="markers", name=goal,
                                 showlegend=False, marker=dict(size=20, color=GREEN if kept else GRAY,
                                                               symbol="circle" if kept else "x")))
        x, y, text = CORNER_TEXT[goal]
        fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=text, showarrow=False, font=dict(size=14, color="black" if kept else GRAY))


Python note. fill="toself" fills the shape that the points of the trace enclose, here the triangle. textangle=60 turns a text by 60 degrees, so that it runs along a side. scaleanchor="x" gives both axes the same scale, so that the triangle keeps its shape, and visible=False hides the axes.


def trilemma(regime="floating exchange rate", di_world=1.0, di_need=0.0):
    """Figure 20.7: the policy trilemma; the foreign rate rises by di_world, the economy needs di_need."""
    di, dE, lost = trilemma_outcome(regime, di_world, di_need)
    flows = "blocked" if regime == "capital controls" else "free"
    fig = go.Figure()
    draw_triangle(fig, regime)
    fig.add_annotation(x=1.0, y=0.62, showarrow=False, align="left", font=dict(size=13, color=BLUE),
                       text=f"Interest rate: {di:+.1f} pt<br>Exchange rate: {dE:+.1f}%<br>Capital flows: {flows}")
    fig.update_xaxes(visible=False, range=[-0.7, 2.7])
    fig.update_yaxes(visible=False, range=[-0.45, 2.1], scaleanchor="x")
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{regime.capitalize()}: Δi = {di:+.1f}, %ΔE = {dE:+.1f}; lost: {lost}")
    return fig


interact(trilemma,
         regime=ToggleButtons(options=["floating exchange rate", "currency board", "capital controls"],
                              value="floating exchange rate", description="regime", style=WIDE),
         di_world=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=-2.0, max=3.0, step=0.5, description="foreign rate rise Δiʷ", style=WIDE),
         di_need=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-2.0, max=3.0, step=0.5, description="rate change the economy needs", style=WIDE));



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Figure 7 with a precomputed slider for the regime
slider_figure(trilemma, "regime", ["floating exchange rate", "currency board", "capital controls"],
              start="floating exchange rate", label="regime")


What to notice.

The Fed raises its rate by 1 point and your economy needs no change. With a floating rate you keep your interest rate, and your currency depreciates by 5 percent: the United States today.
With a currency board the exchange rate stays put, but your interest rate must rise by 1 point although your economy did not need it: Argentina in 1991–2001.
With capital controls you keep both, but only by blocking the free trade in your currency: China in 1996–2005.
Set the needed change equal to the foreign one: then the currency board costs nothing. The trilemma bites only when your economy needs a different policy from the anchor country.

Your turn. A currency board that runs out of foreign reserves cannot hold the peg. Use trilemma_outcome to compare the currency board with a floating rate when the foreign rate rises by 2 points and the economy needs a cut of 1 point. Which goal does each regime sacrifice, and by how much?


Hint

trilemma_outcome("currency board", 2.0, -1.0) and trilemma_outcome("floating exchange rate", 2.0, -1.0). The first gives the rate the economy gets; compare it with the one it needs.

text:
Figure 8: Depreciations during several currency crises
Goal. See how quickly a currency can collapse when a fixed exchange rate breaks down.
Each line is the dollar value of a currency, as an index with 1991 = 100: national currency per dollar in 1991 divided by national currency per dollar in each year (end of year). A fall to 40 means the currency buys only 40 percent of the dollars it bought in 1991.

crises = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig20-8.csv")
crises.head()

The data go to 2025, beyond the textbook’s 1991–2004. By 2025 the Argentine peso is worth 0.07 percent of its 1991 dollar value, so on the textbook’s linear scale its line sits on zero. A ratio scale fixes this: equal distances are then equal percentage changes, so 100 → 10 looks the same as 1 → 0.1.

Python note. updatemenus adds buttons to the figure itself. Each button runs relayout with new axis settings, so it works in Colab and on the website alike. On a log axis Plotly wants the range as powers of ten, which is why we write np.log10(...).


CRISIS_NAMES = {"argentina": "Argentina", "korea": "South Korea", "mexico": "Mexico", "indonesia": "Indonesia"}
long = crises.rename(columns=CRISIS_NAMES).melt(id_vars="year", var_name="country", value_name="index")
fig = px.line(long, x="year", y="index", color="country", hover_name="country", markers=True,
              range_x=[1990.5, 2004.5], range_y=[0, 120],
              labels={"year": "Year", "index": "Dollar value of the currency (1991 = 100)", "country": ""},
              title="Currency crises: four currencies against the dollar (1991 = 100)")
fig.add_vline(x=2004, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
textbook = {"xaxis.range": [1990.5, 2004.5], "yaxis.type": "linear", "yaxis.range": [0, 120], "yaxis.tickvals": None}
latest_linear = {"xaxis.range": [1990.5, 2025.5], "yaxis.type": "linear", "yaxis.range": [0, 120], "yaxis.tickvals": None}
latest_ratio = {"xaxis.range": [1990.5, 2025.5], "yaxis.type": "log", "yaxis.tickvals": [0.1, 1, 10, 100],
                "yaxis.range": [float(np.log10(0.04)), float(np.log10(150))]}
fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=120), updatemenus=[dict(type="buttons", direction="right", x=0, y=1.02,
                                                        xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", buttons=[
    dict(label="1991–2004 (textbook)", method="relayout", args=[textbook]),
    dict(label="1991–2025", method="relayout", args=[latest_linear]),
    dict(label="1991–2025, ratio scale", method="relayout", args=[latest_ratio])])])
fig.show()

What to notice.

Mexico 1994–95: after a year of defending the peg with its reserves, the peso fell to 40 percent of its value.
Asia 1997–98: the Korean won lost about half of its dollar value in 1997, and the Indonesian rupiah fell to a quarter of its 1991 value by 1998.
Argentina 2002: after ten years at exactly 1 peso per dollar, the currency board ended and the peso fell to a third.
Press the buttons. Since 2004 the won and the Mexican peso have drifted lower, while the Argentine peso kept collapsing: only the ratio scale shows that it lost most of its value again and again.


Key numbers: the size of each crisis

moments = crises.set_index("year").rename(columns=CRISIS_NAMES)
for country, year in [("Mexico", 1995), ("South Korea", 1997), ("Indonesia", 1998), ("Argentina", 2002)]:
    value = moments.loc[year, country]
    print(f"{country}, {year}: index {value:.1f}, a loss of {100 - value:.0f}% of the 1991 dollar value")
print(f"Argentina, 2025: index {moments.loc[2025, 'Argentina']:.2f}")

These are the textbook’s numbers, with one exception: Korea’s index in 1997 is 53.8 here and about 45 in the textbook. The won was extremely volatile in the last days of December 1997, so the “end-of-year” rate depends on the exact day and source; the IMF’s current data record a less extreme rate than the vintage the textbook used.
Your turn. In which year did the Mexican peso reach its lowest dollar value, and what is that value?

moments.Mexico.idxmin() gives the year, and moments.Mexico.min() the value.

text:
Figure 9: 10-year government bond yields in Europe
Goal. See the euro crisis in its most useful single graph: interest rates on government debt in Germany, Italy and Spain.
Before the euro, Italian and Spanish bonds paid much more than German ones, mostly because inflation was higher there. With one currency and one central bank, investors expected similar inflation, and the yields converged. After the global financial crisis they diverged again, this time because investors feared a default on sovereign debt.

yields = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig20-9.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
yields.tail(3)

The last Italian value (September 2026) is not published yet, so we drop it after melt.

long = yields.rename(columns={"yield_de": "Germany", "yield_es": "Spain", "yield_it": "Italy"})
long = long.melt(id_vars="date", var_name="country", value_name="yield").dropna()
fig = px.line(long, x="date", y="yield", color="country", hover_name="country", range_y=[-2, 14],
              color_discrete_map={"Germany": BLUE, "Spain": TEAL, "Italy": GREEN},
              labels={"date": "Year", "yield": "10-year government bond yield (percent)", "country": ""},
              title="Bond yields converged with the euro in 1999 and diverged in 2010–2012")
fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
for date, text in [("1999-01-01", "euro"), ("2012-07-01", "Draghi")]:
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=date, x1=date, y0=0, y1=1, yref="paper", line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dot"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=date, y=13, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(color=GRAY))
fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
fig.show()

What to notice.

In 1995 Italy and Spain paid 4 to 6 points more than Germany. By the end of 1998 all three yields were close to 4 percent, and they moved together until 2008.
In 2011–2012 the Italian yield rose above 7 percent and the Spanish one to 6.8 percent, while Germany’s fell. After Mario Draghi promised in July 2012 that the ECB would do “whatever it takes”, the gaps closed again.
German yields were negative in 2016 and in 2019–2021: investors paid the German government to hold their money.


Key numbers: the spreads over Germany
The spread is the gap between a country’s yield and Germany’s. It measures how much more investors want to be paid to lend to that government.

text:
Figure 10: Domestic bank lending in Europe
Goal. See the credit boom in southern Europe after the euro arrived.
The data are lending by domestic banks to the private sector, in percent of GDP, for the textbook’s three years plus the latest year, 2023.

lending = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig20-10.csv")
lending


Python note. melt stacks the four year columns into one column of values, with a new column that says which year each value belongs to. .map(YEARS) replaces the column names by readable labels. barmode="group" puts the bars of the four years side by side.


YEARS = {"credit_gdp_1998": "1998", "credit_gdp_2002": "2002", "credit_gdp_2007": "2007",
         "credit_gdp_2023": "2023 (latest)"}
bars = lending.melt(id_vars=["iso3", "country"], value_vars=list(YEARS), var_name="year", value_name="credit")
bars["year"] = bars.year.map(YEARS)
fig = px.bar(bars, x="country", y="credit", color="year", barmode="group", hover_name="country",
             color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8"], range_y=[0, 200],
             labels={"country": "", "credit": "Domestic bank lending (percent of GDP)", "year": ""},
             title="Bank lending boomed in southern Europe after the euro, and has shrunk since")
fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
fig.show()

What to notice.

From 1998 to 2007 bank lending rose from 32 to 84 percent of GDP in Greece and from 83 to 168 percent in Spain. In Germany it fell.
The 2023 bars show the hangover: after the crisis, lending fell back, to 25 percent of GDP in Ireland.


Data revisions: the same years, different numbers
The textbook’s figure comes from a 2010 edition of the World Bank’s database. Today’s edition revises some bars.

book = pd.DataFrame({"country": ["Greece", "Ireland", "Portugal", "Spain", "Italy", "Germany"],
                     "textbook_2007": [84, 184, 159, 168, 96, 105]})
revisions = lending[["country", "credit_gdp_2007"]].merge(book, on="country")
revisions["revision"] = revisions.credit_gdp_2007 - revisions.textbook_2007
revisions.round(1)

Greece and Spain are unchanged, but Ireland’s 2007 lending is now 26 points lower. The story, a boom in the south after the euro, survives the revisions.

text:
Figure 11: Current account balances in Europe
Goal. See that northern Europe lent to southern Europe after the euro: the borrowing came from abroad, too.
The current account balance is the trade balance plus the interest and dividends a country earns on its past lending abroad (minus those it pays). A deficit means the country borrows from the rest of the world. Each bar is the average over a period, in percent of GDP.

current = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig20-11.csv")
PERIODS = {"ca_gdp_1993_1997": "1993–1997", "ca_gdp_2003_2007": "2003–2007", "ca_gdp_2008_2011": "2008–2011",
           "ca_gdp_2021_2025": "2021–2025 (latest)"}
bars = current.melt(id_vars=["iso3", "country"], value_vars=list(PERIODS), var_name="period", value_name="balance")
bars["period"] = bars.period.map(PERIODS)
fig = px.bar(bars, x="country", y="balance", color="period", barmode="group", hover_name="country",
             color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8"], range_y=[-14, 14],
             labels={"country": "", "balance": "Current account balance (percent of GDP)", "period": ""},
             title="Current accounts: the south borrowed abroad after the euro, Germany lent")
fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
fig.show()

What to notice.

Greece borrowed 2 percent of its GDP a year from abroad in 1993–97 and 9 percent in 2003–07; Spain went from about 1 to 7 percent. Germany turned from a small deficit into a surplus of about 5 percent of GDP.
Since 2021 Portugal, Spain and Italy have small surpluses; Greece still borrows 7.5 percent of GDP.

Key numbers: the interest bill on a debt of 100 percent of GDP
A government with debt \(D\) must pay interest \(R \cdot D\) every year, so the interest bill in percent of GDP is the debt-GDP ratio times the interest rate. If investors fear a default and ask for a higher rate, the bill grows, which makes a default more likely: the crisis can be self-fulfilling.

def interest_bill(debt_ratio, R):
    """Yearly interest payments in percent of GDP: debt-GDP ratio (percent) times the interest rate (percent)."""
    return debt_ratio * R / 100
